title: Soft Deletes, Archive Tables and History Tables
objectives: Weigh soft deletes against hard deletes, including their effect on constraints and queries
Decide whether deleted rows stay in place or move to an archive table
Keep row versions in a history table and query a value as it was at a past moment

cards.title: Deleted, or just hidden?
cards.body: A hard delete removes the row. A soft delete sets a column such as deleted_at and every query filters those rows out. Soft deletes make undo a one-row update, keep old orders pointing at a real customer row, and leave evidence for support. They also cost something: every query must remember the filter, unique constraints still see the hidden rows, and the table keeps growing with rows that ordinary queries never return.

cards.title: Worked example: the email that cannot be reused
cards.body: Soft deletes interact with unique constraints in a way that surprises most teams the first time.
steps: users has a unique constraint on email and a nullable deleted_at column
Ann closes her account: deleted_at is set and the row stays
A month later she signs up again with the same email, and the unique constraint rejects it
Fix: replace the constraint with a unique index on email WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, so only live rows compete
Do not reach for UNIQUE (email, deleted_at): live rows all have a NULL deleted_at, and NULLs never count as equal, so two live accounts could share an email

cards.title: Where deleted rows live
cards.body: A deleted_at column keeps deleted rows in place: a restore is one UPDATE, and foreign keys from old orders stay valid. But hidden rows still fill the table's pages, so a table where most rows are deleted spends most of every scan and most of its cached pages on rows nobody asked for. Partial indexes WHERE deleted_at IS NULL keep the indexes small, but not the table. The alternative is an archive table with the same columns. One statement moves the row, for example WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM projects WHERE id = 7 RETURNING *) INSERT INTO projects_archive SELECT * FROM gone, so the live table holds only live rows and queries need no filter. The price: no foreign key can point at an archived row, and a restore is the same move in reverse.

cards.title: A history table with valid time
cards.body: Some questions need the value as it was, not just whether a row exists: the price on the invoice date, the address at the time of shipping.
steps: prices_history(product_id, price, valid_from, valid_to), where an open valid_to means current
A price change closes the current row (valid_to = now) and inserts the new price with an open valid_to, in one transaction
Price on 3 March: the row where valid_from <= '2026-03-03' and (valid_to > '2026-03-03' or valid_to IS NULL)
A unique index on product_id WHERE valid_to IS NULL allows one current row; an exclusion constraint stops any two periods from overlapping
An index on (product_id, valid_from) finds the right version quickly; SQL Server and MariaDB system-versioned tables do this bookkeeping for you, PostgreSQL needs triggers

cards.title: Trap: the forgotten filter
cards.body: With soft deletes, correctness depends on every query adding deleted_at IS NULL. One dashboard, export or join that forgets it counts deleted customers or emails people who left. Put the filter where queries cannot skip it: a view over live rows that the application reads from, or a row-level security policy. Keep direct access to the base table for the few jobs that genuinely need deleted rows.

cards.title: Edge case: two changes at the same moment
cards.body: Two sessions change product 5's price at once. Each closes "the current row" and inserts its own new price, and if nothing stops them the table ends up with two open versions, so the current price has two answers. Serialise changes per key, for example by locking product 5's row in products with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before touching its history. And let the schema refuse the bad state anyway: a unique index on product_id WHERE valid_to IS NULL allows only one current version, and in PostgreSQL an exclusion constraint such as EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, tstzrange(valid_from, valid_to) WITH &&), which needs the btree_gist extension, rejects any two overlapping periods.

questions.prompt: Soft-deleted users keep appearing in the “active users” dashboard and in two exports. Which fix holds up as new queries are written?

choices.label: Add deleted_at IS NULL to the dashboard and both exports
Point the dashboard and exports at a view of live users
Cache the user list and drop deleted users from the cache
Add an index on deleted_at so the filter runs faster

questions.explanation: A view that already applies the filter makes the safe query the easy one, so new reports inherit it. Patching three queries fixes today's bug, but the next query written against the table can forget the filter again. A cache adds a second copy to keep correct and leaves the database queries unfixed. An index speeds up the filter but does not add it to queries that lack it.

questions.prompt: To let deleted users rejoin, a team replaced UNIQUE (email) with UNIQUE (email, deleted_at). A week later two live accounts share one email. Why?

choices.label: Live rows have NULL deleted_at, and NULLs never equal each other
The constraint is only checked when deleted_at itself changes value
Unique constraints skip rows that were inserted in the same second
The two sign-ups committed in different transactions

questions.explanation: A unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct by default, so (ann@example.com, NULL) and (ann@example.com, NULL) do not conflict. Use a unique index on email WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, so only live rows compete; PostgreSQL 15 and later also offer UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT. Unique constraints are checked on every insert and on updates of any of their columns, with no time window, and they work across transactions; that is their whole purpose.

questions.prompt: Two price changes for product 5 ran at the same moment, and prices_history now has two rows with an open valid_to. Which rule would have rejected the second one?

choices.label: A unique index on product_id WHERE valid_to IS NULL
An index on (product_id, valid_from) for faster lookups
A CHECK that valid_to is later than valid_from
Running both changes at Read Committed isolation

questions.explanation: The partial unique index lets each product have only one row with an open valid_to, so the second insert fails and that change can retry. The lookup index speeds up queries but enforces nothing. A CHECK sees one row at a time, and both rows pass it. Read Committed is the usual default and does not stop two transactions from inserting rows that conflict only in meaning.

questions.prompt: prices_history stores (product_id, price, valid_from, valid_to), with an open valid_to for the current price. Which row gives product 5's price on 3 March?

choices.label: The row with the largest valid_from value stored for product 5
The row whose valid_from to valid_to period covers 3 March
The row whose valid_to equals 3 March
The row whose valid_from equals 3 March

questions.explanation: A version applies from valid_from up to, but not including, valid_to, so the right row is the one whose period covers 3 March, counting an open valid_to as running to now. The largest valid_from is today's price, not the price on that date. Matching valid_to or valid_from exactly finds a row only if the price happened to change that day.

questions.prompt: A projects table gains 40,000 rows a day, and 35,000 projects a day are soft-deleted. Nothing is ever purged. After two years, roughly what percentage of its rows are live?
questions.explanation: Design implication: seven rows in eight are hidden, and every scan and cached page carries them. Partial indexes keep the indexes small, but the table needs an archive table or a purge. 87.5 is the deleted share, and 14.3 divides live rows by deletes instead of by all rows.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that change product 5's price in prices_history, which has a unique index on product_id WHERE valid_to IS NULL.

items.label: Set valid_to = now() on product 5's open history row
COMMIT, so readers see both rows change at once
BEGIN a transaction
Insert the new price with valid_from = now() and an open valid_to
Lock product 5's row in products with FOR UPDATE

questions.explanation: The lock serialises changes to one product, so two changes cannot both close the same version. The old version must be closed before the new one is inserted, or the unique index sees two open rows. In PostgreSQL now() is fixed for the whole transaction, so the old period ends exactly where the new one starts, and COMMIT publishes both rows together.

questions.prompt: A projects table has grown to 30 million rows, 26 million of them soft-deleted. Live queries touch only live projects, restores happen a few times a month, and no other table references deleted projects.

approaches.label: Hard delete
approaches.description: Delete rows outright and restore from backups when asked

approaches.label: Keep deleted_at
approaches.description: Leave deleted rows in place and add partial indexes on live rows

approaches.label: Archive table
approaches.description: Move deleted rows to projects_archive in the deleting statement, and back to restore

rationaleOptions.label: Partial indexes also shrink the table that scans have to read
The live table and its indexes hold only the 4 million live rows
Restoring one project from a full backup is quick and precise
Deleting and restoring are each one atomic move between two tables

rationaleConflicts.r3: Partial indexes shrink only the indexes; the 26 million hidden rows still fill the table pages that scans and the cache read.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A backup restore brings back a whole database as of one moment; pulling out one project and its children by hand is slow and error-prone.

questions.explanation: With most rows deleted and nothing referencing them, moving them out keeps the busy table small and removes the filter from every query. If other tables did reference deleted projects, deleted_at in place would be the better choice.

flashcards.back: Mark a row deleted instead of removing it; filter it from queries, mind unique constraints
Use a unique index on email WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
Deleted rows moved out in the same statement; the live table stays small, but nothing can reference them
The database keeps old row versions and answers AS OF queries; SQL Server and MariaDB have them

mechanism.title: What each way of keeping the past stores, and what it costs
steps: A hard delete removes the row and, through foreign keys, either blocks the delete, cascades to children or nulls references. The data is gone except in backups. It is the simplest option and the right one for data nobody needs to recover.

A soft delete flags the row instead. Undo is one update, references stay valid, and support can see what happened. But the row still takes part in unique constraints and joins, and the flag becomes part of every query. A view or row-level policy over live rows keeps that filter in one place.

An archive table moves deleted rows out instead. A data-modifying statement deletes from the live table and inserts into the archive in one step, so the live table and its indexes hold only live rows and need no filter. Nothing can reference an archived row, so it suits entities whose references are gone or were never kept.

A history table keeps whole row versions with a validity interval, valid_from and valid_to, so it answers “what was the value at time T?”. Each change closes the current version and opens a new one in one transaction. A partial unique index on the key WHERE valid_to IS NULL allows one current version, an exclusion constraint stops periods from overlapping, and an index on (key, valid_from) makes point-in-time lookups fast.

System-versioned tables, from the SQL:2011 standard, do this bookkeeping in the engine and add AS OF query syntax. SQL Server and MariaDB support them; in PostgreSQL the same effect needs triggers or an extension.

All of these keep data longer, and growth is the bill. A table where most rows are hidden, or a history table with a version per change, needs a purge, archive or partitioning plan from day one. Which data must be erased, and when, is a retention policy decided by the application; the schema should make carrying it out a simple delete.

useWhen: Users or support need undo for a while after a delete
Other rows must keep pointing at the deleted entity, such as orders of a closed account
Most rows end up deleted and nothing references them: move them to an archive table
Invoices, prices or addresses must be reproduced exactly as they were at a past time
avoidWhen: The data has no recovery value, such as expired sessions or temporary tokens
Tables are huge and churn fast, so keeping every deleted row would dominate storage
Other tables must keep referencing deleted rows: an archive table would break those foreign keys
A full history of every row version would cost more than the questions it answers

rows: What existed and when it was removed
Every query needs the filter; unique constraints need care
What was deleted, kept out of the live table
No foreign keys to archived rows; restore is a move
The value at any past moment
One row version per change, plus interval queries

numbers.title: How much of a never-purged table is live
steps: Rows written: 40,000 × 730 = 29.2 million.
Live rows: (40,000 − 35,000) × 730 = 3.65 million, which is 12.5%.
Seven rows in eight that a scan reads, and that cached pages hold, are hidden rows.
Partial indexes keep the indexes near the size of the 3.65 million live rows; the table itself needs an archive table or a purge.
numbers.result: A soft-delete table that is never purged becomes mostly dead weight; decide early where deleted rows go and when they leave.

india.title: SQL Server temporal tables and PostgreSQL exclusion constraints
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft's documentation on temporal tables describes system-versioned tables: the engine moves each old row version into a history table with period columns and supports FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF, BETWEEN and ALL queries. The PostgreSQL manual's section on exclusion constraints explains that EXCLUDE guarantees no two rows satisfy all the listed operator comparisons, which with = on the key and && on a range type means no two versions of one key overlap in time.

pitfalls.trap: UNIQUE(email, deleted_at) to allow re-registration
pitfalls.say: NULLs are distinct, so live duplicates slip through; use a partial unique index

pitfalls.trap: Closing and opening versions without a per-key lock
pitfalls.say: Two concurrent changes leave two open rows; lock the key and add a partial unique index

pitfalls.trap: Keeping soft-deleted and history rows forever
pitfalls.say: Plan a purge, archive table or partitions so growth stays bounded

takeaways: Soft deletes give undo, but every query and unique constraint must account for them
Put the live-rows filter in one place: a view or a row-level policy
Move mostly-deleted, unreferenced rows to an archive table
Change history rows under a lock, with a partial unique index or exclusion constraint as the backstop

interactive.title: Where should the filter live?
interactive.prompt: An app has 40 queries over customers, and soft-deleted customers must never appear except in two admin tools. New reports are added every month. Where should the deleted_at IS NULL filter live?

choices.label: In each query, checked during code review
choices.feedback: Review catches most cases, but one miss leaks deleted customers, and the risk grows with every new report.

choices.label: In a view or row-level policy that ordinary queries go through
choices.feedback: Right: the safe path is the default, and only the admin tools read the base table.

choices.label: In a cache layer that drops deleted customers
choices.feedback: A cache hides the problem for some reads while direct queries stay wrong.

interactive.reveal: Correctness that depends on every author remembering a filter fails eventually. Make the filtered view the thing queries use, and grant base-table access only where deleted rows are needed.

seeAlso.why: Keys, constraints and delete actions, which soft deletes change
Partial indexes, which keep soft-deleted rows out of unique and lookup indexes
Partitioning, which turns purging old history into dropping a partition
Deleting data across a service: cascades, tombstones and deletion workflows
Audit trails in code: who acted, impersonation and activity logs
Tamper-evident security logging, including audit rows written by database triggers

title: Materialised Views and Summary Tables
objectives: Tell a view from a materialised view, and estimate what precomputing saves
Choose between full refresh, concurrent refresh and incremental maintenance
Reason about staleness, hot summary rows and late corrections

cards.title: Compute once, read many times
cards.body: A view is a saved query: every read runs it again. A materialised view stores the result as a table, so reads are as fast as reading any small table, but the data is only as fresh as the last refresh. A summary table is the hand-built version: a table of totals that your own code or jobs keep up to date. Both trade freshness and some extra writes for much cheaper reads, which pays off when the same expensive aggregate is read again and again.

cards.title: Worked example: a dashboard that scans 500 million rows
cards.body: Count the work per hour before and after, including the cost of refreshing.
steps: Assume the sales dashboard aggregates 500 million order lines in 40 s, and 200 people open it each hour (illustrative)
Live: 200 × 40 s = 8,000 s of database work an hour, more than two cores busy all the time
Materialised daily totals per store: 2,000 stores × 1,500 days = 3 million rows; a dashboard read takes about 50 ms
A full refresh every 15 minutes at 40 s each: 4 × 40 s = 160 s an hour
Total: 160 s of refresh plus 200 × 0.05 s = 10 s of reads, about 170 s an hour instead of 8,000 s

cards.title: Full, concurrent and incremental refresh
cards.body: A full refresh reruns the whole query. In PostgreSQL, plain REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW locks out readers while it runs; with CONCURRENTLY, readers keep the old contents while the new result is computed and the differences are applied, which needs a unique index on the view and costs more work. Incremental maintenance changes only what is affected: each new order adds its amount to its day's row, in the same transaction or from a change stream. Some engines do this for certain views: SQL Server indexed views are maintained with every change to the base tables, and Oracle materialised views can fast-refresh from change logs.

cards.title: Misconception: “a view makes the query fast”
cards.body: A plain view is stored text, not stored results. Selecting from a view of a 30-second report takes about 30 seconds, every time. What a plain view buys is one definition that every caller shares. Speed comes only from storing results, in a materialised view or a summary table, or from indexes that make the underlying query fast.

cards.title: Trap: a hot summary row
cards.body: Incremental totals put many writers on very few rows. If every order updates today's total for its store, a busy store's orders all wait for one row lock, and checkout throughput is capped by how fast that one row can be updated and committed. Spread the hot spot: append each order's amount to a small deltas table and roll it up every minute, or split the counter into several rows and add them up when reading.

cards.title: Edge case: late and corrected data
cards.body: A refund recorded three days after the sale, or an event that arrives late from an offline device, changes totals that were already summarised. A full refresh picks the change up automatically. An incremental summary must apply it as its own correction, such as a negative amount for the original day. A common safety net is a scheduled job that recomputes the last few days from the base data, so any drift is bounded.

questions.prompt: A team wraps a slow 30-second report in a plain, non-materialised view. How long does SELECT * FROM the view take?

choices.label: Milliseconds, because views store their last result
About 30 seconds, because the view runs the query each time
About 15 seconds, because views skip the final sort
It depends on how recently the view was last refreshed by a job

questions.explanation: A plain view is a stored query definition, so reading it runs the same 30-second query. Storing results is what a materialised view does, and only materialised views have a refresh. A view does not drop the sort; the planner runs the same plan it would for the query written out in full.

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL's REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY require a unique index on the view?

choices.label: To lock the base tables against writes during the rebuild
To match old and new rows so it can apply only the differences
Because the unique index speeds up the aggregate query itself
To stop two refreshes of the same view from overlapping

questions.explanation: A concurrent refresh computes the new result, compares it with the current contents row by row, and applies inserts, updates and deletes, so readers keep seeing a complete view. Matching rows needs a unique key. It does not lock base tables against writes, the index is on the view, not used by the source query, and overlapping refreshes are prevented by a lock, not by the index.

questions.prompt: A summary starts a full refresh every 10 minutes, and each refresh takes 2 minutes. Each refresh reads the base data as of the moment it starts. At worst, how many minutes old is the data a reader sees?
assumptions: Each refresh reads data as of its start
questions.workedAnswer: A refresh starting at 0:00 shows data as of 0:00 until the next one finishes at 0:12: 10 + 2 = 12 minutes
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the worst moment is just before the next refresh completes. Answering 10 ignores the time the refresh itself takes, and 8 subtracts it instead of adding it.

questions.prompt: Each order adds its amount to one daily_totals row for its store. During a flash sale, one store gets 2,000 orders a second and its checkouts slow down. Why?

choices.label: The summary table needs a larger index on store_id
The materialised view refreshes after each insert
Every order waits for the lock on the same summary row
The totals column overflows its integer type at that write rate

questions.explanation: All 2,000 orders a second update one row, and each update holds that row's lock until its transaction commits, so they queue behind each other. An index helps find the row, not share it. There is no view refresh here, since this is a summary table maintained by each order. Numeric columns do not overflow from a high rate, only from large values.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a correct incremental daily-total update in order.

items.label: Add its amount to that day's total with an atomic UPDATE … SET total = total + amount
A scheduled job recomputes recent days from base data and repairs any drift
BEGIN a transaction
COMMIT the order and the total together
Insert the order row

questions.explanation: The order and the total change in one transaction, so a crash leaves neither half-applied. The atomic UPDATE avoids a read-then-write race between concurrent orders. The scheduled recompute catches corrections and bugs that slipped past the incremental path.

questions.prompt: A leaderboard shows the top 100 users by total points out of 10 million users. Points change constantly, and the page may be up to a minute stale.
constraints: Up to a minute of staleness is fine

approaches.label: Aggregate the full points log on every page view
approaches.description: Always fresh

approaches.label: Refresh a materialised view after every point awarded
approaches.description: Refresh on each write

approaches.label: A summary of the top users, refreshed every minute
approaches.description: Periodic summary

rationaleOptions.label: Refreshing after every point keeps the view cheap to maintain
A minute of allowed staleness fits a periodic refresh
Aggregating on every read works at any data size
Each page view reads 100 precomputed rows

rationaleConflicts.r3: A full refresh per point repeats the whole aggregate thousands of times a second.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Aggregating 10 million users' points per page view is the expensive query the summary exists to avoid.

questions.explanation: The allowed staleness is the budget that makes precomputing possible. At larger scale or tighter freshness, an in-memory sorted set is the usual next step.

flashcards.back: A view reruns its query on every read; a materialised view stores the result until refreshed
PostgreSQL: readers keep the old contents during refresh; needs a unique index on the view
Refresh interval plus refresh duration

mechanism.title: How precomputed results are built, refreshed and read
steps: A plain view stores a query. Reading it substitutes the query into the caller's statement, so it costs exactly as much as running the query. It is a tool for sharing one definition, not for speed.

A materialised view runs the query once and stores the result rows in a table. Reads scan or index that stored table, which can be millions of times smaller than the base data. You can add indexes to it like any table.

A full refresh reruns the query and replaces the contents. Plain refresh in PostgreSQL blocks readers while it runs; a concurrent refresh builds the new result, compares it with the old using a unique index, and applies only the changed rows, so reads continue. Either way, the data is as of when the refresh started.

Incremental maintenance updates only the affected summary rows whenever base data changes, either in the same transaction as the change or by consuming a change stream. Some engines do it for restricted kinds of views; otherwise you write it yourself as a summary table. It is fresh, but every write pays, and popular rows become lock hot spots.
Corrections and late data must reach the summary too. A full refresh handles them automatically. Incremental paths need explicit corrections, and a periodic recompute of recent days bounds any drift.

Choose by the freshness you need and the read-to-write ratio. Minutes of staleness and heavy reads favour periodic refresh. Seconds of staleness favour incremental updates. If neither the read rate nor the query cost is high, a good index on the base table may be enough.

useWhen: The same expensive aggregate is read far more often than the base data changes
Readers accept data that is minutes old, such as dashboards and reports
A totals table can be updated in the same transaction as each change, for real-time counts
You want an indexed, queryable snapshot for a downstream job
avoidWhen: Readers need every change reflected the instant it commits and the base query is cheap enough to run
A full refresh takes longer than the allowed staleness
Many writers would update the same few summary rows at high rates
The query is rarely read, so a refresh costs more than it saves

rows: As of the last refresh start
As of the last refresh start

numbers.title: Database work per hour for the dashboard
assumptions: Query takes 40 s over 500 million rows
steps: Live: 200 × 40 s = 8,000 s an hour, about 2.2 cores busy (8,000 ÷ 3,600).
Refresh: 4 × 40 s = 160 s an hour.
Reads: 200 × 0.05 s = 10 s an hour.
Total: 160 + 10 = 170 s, about 47 times less work (8,000 ÷ 170).
numbers.result: The summary cuts database work by about 47 times and makes the page load in milliseconds, at the price of data up to about 15 minutes plus one refresh old.

india.title: PostgreSQL and SQL Server documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual for REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW explains that a concurrent refresh lets selects continue during the refresh, requires at least one unique index on the view covering all rows, and can be slower when many rows change. Microsoft's documentation on indexed views explains that SQL Server stores the view's result in a clustered index and maintains it as the base tables change, with restrictions on which query constructs are allowed.

pitfalls.trap: Using a plain view to speed up a slow report
pitfalls.say: A view reruns the query; store the results to save work

pitfalls.trap: Incrementing one summary row from every write
pitfalls.say: Hot rows serialise writers; append deltas or split the counter

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring late corrections in incremental summaries
pitfalls.say: Apply corrections explicitly and recompute recent days on a schedule

takeaways: A view saves typing; a materialised view saves work
Worst-case staleness is the refresh interval plus the refresh time
Incremental summaries are fresh but put every writer on a few hot rows
Late and corrected data needs a plan: recompute recent periods on a schedule

interactive.title: What does the dashboard show?
interactive.prompt: A materialised view of daily sales totals refreshes at 02:00 each night. A refund for yesterday's sale is recorded at 10:00 today. What does the dashboard show for yesterday at 15:00?

choices.label: The corrected total, because the view tracks its base tables
choices.feedback: Only plain views and engine-maintained indexed views track changes; this one waits for its refresh.

choices.label: An error, because its base data changed after the refresh
choices.feedback: Changed base data does not invalidate a materialised view; it just makes it stale.

choices.label: Yesterday's total without the refund, until the next refresh at 02:00
choices.feedback: Right: the view holds the result computed at 02:00 today.

interactive.reveal: Staleness is the contract of a refreshed view. Show users when it was last refreshed, and refresh more often or maintain totals incrementally if that gap is not acceptable.

seeAlso.why: Warehouses and OLAP systems take precomputed aggregates much further
Normal forms explain the update anomalies that copied totals reintroduce
Normalization versus denormalization, the trade-off every stored summary makes

title: Multi-Tenant Data Models and Row-Level Security
objectives: Compare shared tables, schema per tenant and database per tenant as data layouts
Put tenant_id in keys, foreign keys and indexes so the schema itself keeps tenants apart
Set up row-level security so a query that forgets the tenant filter cannot leak rows

cards.title: One application, many customers
cards.body: A software-as-a-service product keeps data for many customer organisations, called tenants. There are three main layouts. Shared tables put every tenant in the same tables, with a tenant_id column on every row. A schema or database per tenant gives each its own copy of the tables on shared servers. A dedicated database server per tenant isolates them fully. The layout also decides per-tenant operations: with a database per tenant, restoring one tenant to an hour ago is an ordinary point-in-time restore; with shared tables it means restoring a copy elsewhere and copying that tenant's rows back table by table.

cards.title: Worked example: what each model costs at 5,000 tenants
cards.body: Most tenants are small. The layout decision is mostly about operations, not storage.
steps: Assume 5,000 tenants, 30 tables and 50 indexes per copy of the schema, and 20 large tenants holding half the data (illustrative)
Shared tables: one schema, so each migration runs once, and the catalog holds 80 tables and indexes
Schema per tenant: each migration runs 5,000 times, and the catalog holds 5,000 × 80 = 400,000 tables and indexes
Server per tenant: 5,000 databases to patch, back up, monitor and pay for
Hybrid: shared tables for the long tail, dedicated databases for the few large or regulated tenants

cards.title: tenant_id in keys and constraints
cards.body: In shared tables, the schema can carry the tenant. Unique rules include it: emails unique within a company means UNIQUE (tenant_id, email), not UNIQUE (email). Foreign keys between tenant tables include it too. If invoices has UNIQUE (tenant_id, id), then invoice_lines can declare FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, invoice_id) REFERENCES invoices (tenant_id, id), and a line can no longer point at another tenant's invoice; a key on invoice_id alone only checks that the invoice exists somewhere. Joins between tenant tables match on tenant_id as well as the id, so the planner and the constraints agree.

cards.title: Row-level security as a backstop
cards.body: Row-level security makes the database add a filter to every query on a table. In PostgreSQL, a policy such as USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint) means a query that forgets WHERE tenant_id = … sees only the current tenant's rows instead of everyone's; a policy for all commands also applies that condition to rows being inserted or updated. SQL Server has an equivalent feature. Two details matter. In PostgreSQL, the table owner bypasses policies unless the table is set to FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and superusers always bypass them, so the application should connect as a separate, ordinary role. And the tenant setting must be set for each transaction, from the tenant the server derived when it authenticated the request; behind a transaction pooler, use SET LOCAL so it cannot leak to the next client.

cards.title: Trap: indexes that do not start with tenant_id
cards.body: An index on (created_at) looks right for "tenant 42's 20 newest invoices", but every tenant's rows are interleaved in it. The database walks the newest entries of all tenants and throws away each one that is not tenant 42's; for a small tenant whose last invoice was months ago, that can mean most of the index. An index on (tenant_id, created_at) jumps straight to tenant 42's slice and reads 20 entries. Lead primary keys and indexes with tenant_id. The tenant_id = … condition that a row-level security policy adds can use such an index like any other condition.

cards.title: Edge case: moving a tenant between databases
cards.body: A large tenant outgrows the shared tables and moves to its own database, or a small one moves back. If ids come from a sequence per database, the tenant's invoice 9001 may already exist in the target, and fixing that means renumbering every row and every foreign key that points at it. Keys that do not depend on one database's sequence copy across unchanged: UUIDs, or ids scoped to the tenant under a (tenant_id, id) key. With tenant_id in every table, extracting a tenant is the same WHERE tenant_id = 42 on each table, and the cutover is a change to connection routing.

questions.prompt: In shared tables, emails must be unique within each company, but two companies may have users with the same email. Which constraint fits?

choices.label: UNIQUE (email)
UNIQUE (tenant_id)
UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)
A unique index on lower(email)

questions.explanation: Uniqueness should be scoped to the tenant, so the constraint covers the pair. UNIQUE (email) and a unique lower(email) index both block the same email at two different companies. UNIQUE (tenant_id) allows only one user per company.

questions.prompt: Row-level security is enabled on a table with a tenant policy, yet a reporting tool that connects as the table owner sees every tenant's rows. Why?

choices.label: Policies apply to SELECT statements only after a restart
The table owner bypasses policies unless the table forces them
Policies are applied only inside stored procedures
The owner's session cached the rows before the policy was added

questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL, owners bypass row-level security by default; ALTER TABLE … FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY applies the policies to the owner too, and superusers always bypass them. Connect applications and tools as an ordinary role instead. Policies take effect without a restart, apply to every query on the table, not just procedures, and there is no row cache that predates them.

questions.prompt: Tenant 42 ran a bad import an hour ago and wants only its own data put back as it was before. Which layout makes that one standard restore?

choices.label: Shared tables, restoring the latest backup over the database
A database per tenant, restored to a point in time
Shared tables with row-level security on every table
Shared tables with indexes that lead with tenant_id

questions.explanation: When the tenant has its own database, a point-in-time restore of that database rewinds tenant 42 and nobody else. Restoring the shared database rewinds every tenant and loses their last hour too; the shared-table route is to restore a copy elsewhere and copy tenant 42's rows back table by table. Row-level security and tenant-leading indexes control reads and their speed, not recovery.

questions.prompt: invoice_lines rows of tenant 7 point at invoice 9001, which belongs to tenant 3. Which rule on invoice_lines, referencing invoices, would have rejected them?

choices.label: A foreign key on invoice_id referencing invoices
A foreign key on (tenant_id, invoice_id)
An index on invoice_lines (tenant_id, invoice_id)
A CHECK that tenant_id is positive

questions.explanation: The composite key requires an invoice with the same tenant_id and id, so a line of tenant 7 cannot reference tenant 3's invoice; invoices needs UNIQUE (tenant_id, id) for it to point at. A key on invoice_id alone only checks that invoice 9001 exists somewhere, which it does. An index speeds up lookups but enforces nothing. A CHECK sees only its own row, and 7 is positive.

questions.prompt: With a schema per tenant, 3,000 tenants each have 40 tables and 60 indexes. How many tables and indexes does the database catalog hold for them?
assumptions: 40 tables and 60 indexes per tenant schema
questions.explanation: Design implication: every one of the 300,000 has its own files, statistics and catalog rows, and each migration must run 3,000 times. 3,000 counts one object per tenant, and 180,000 counts only the indexes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order for a request that reads tenant data with row-level security behind a transaction pooler.

items.label: Run the queries, which the policies filter by tenant
Authenticate the user and look up their tenant on the server
COMMIT, which also clears the setting
SET LOCAL the tenant setting for this transaction
BEGIN a transaction

questions.explanation: The tenant must come from authentication, not the request. SET LOCAL lasts only until the end of the transaction, so when the pooler hands the connection to another client, no tenant setting is left behind. SET LOCAL before BEGIN does nothing at all (PostgreSQL only warns), so the queries would run without the tenant; plain SET would keep it for the whole session, which is exactly what leaks across clients.

questions.prompt: A shared invoices table holds 2,000 tenants. Every screen lists one tenant's recent invoices, and the largest tenants will later move to their own databases.

approaches.label: Global keys
approaches.description: bigint id from one sequence as the primary key, plus an index on created_at

approaches.description: invoices_0001 to invoices_2000, with their own indexes

sources.title: AWS whitepaper: SaaS tenant isolation strategies

mechanism.title: How tenant data is separated, from shared rows to separate servers
steps: Every multi-tenant system answers two questions: where each tenant's rows live, and what stops one tenant from seeing another's. The layouts range from pooled (everyone in the same tables) to siloed (each tenant on its own database), with schema-per-tenant in between.

In shared tables, the schema can carry the tenant. tenant_id is in each row and leads the primary key, unique rules include it, foreign keys between tenant tables include it so a row cannot point at another tenant's row, and joins match on it.

Indexes lead with tenant_id, so one tenant's queries touch only its slice of each index instead of walking past every other tenant's entries. The same holds for the condition a row-level security policy adds.

Row-level security moves the tenant filter into the database. A policy on the table is added to every query from ordinary roles, and the application sets the current tenant for each transaction with SET LOCAL. A forgotten WHERE then returns only the current tenant's rows. It is a backstop: it trusts whatever tenant it is given.

A schema or database per tenant makes isolation structural: a query on one tenant's tables cannot touch another's, and per-tenant restore is a normal restore. The cost is multiplied operations: every migration runs once per tenant, the catalog holds a copy of every table and index for each, and connection routing must pick the right schema or database.

Most products end up hybrid: pooled tables for the many small tenants, and dedicated databases for the few that are very large, regulated or paying for isolation. Keep one schema, and keys that do not depend on one database's sequence, so moving a tenant between the two is a data copy, not a renumbering. Separating data does not separate load: tenants on one server still share its CPU, I/O and connections.

useWhen: Many small tenants with similar needs: shared tables with tenant_id
You want the database to stop cross-tenant reads even when a query is wrong: add row-level security
A few tenants need contractual isolation, their own keys or their own region: give them dedicated databases
Tenants need per-tenant restore or deletion often: separate schemas or databases make that a single operation
avoidWhen: Avoid schema-per-tenant for tens of thousands of tenants; migrations and catalog size explode
Avoid a server per tenant for a long tail of small customers
Avoid foreign keys and indexes that leave tenant_id out
Avoid connecting the application as the table owner or a superuser when relying on row-level security

rows: Keys and queries, plus optional row-level security

india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual's chapter on row security policies explains that once row-level security is enabled, ordinary roles see only rows allowed by a policy, that table owners bypass policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, and that superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS always bypass them. The AWS whitepaper on SaaS tenant isolation strategies describes silo, pool and bridge models, which map to database per tenant, shared tables and the mixed approaches in between, and argues that isolation must be enforced, not just assumed.

title: The Buffer Pool and the Working Set
objectives: Explain how a database caches pages and why the miss rate, not the hit rate, drives latency
Estimate the working set and recognise when it outgrows memory
Plan for large scans and cold caches after restarts and failovers

cards.title: Pages, not rows
cards.body: Databases read and cache whole pages: 8 KB in PostgreSQL and 16 KB by default in InnoDB. The buffer pool (shared_buffers in PostgreSQL, the InnoDB buffer pool in MySQL) keeps recently used pages in memory. A query that needs a row first asks for its page: a hit costs microseconds, a miss means waiting for storage. Changed pages stay in memory as dirty pages until a checkpoint or background writer saves them; the write-ahead log already made the change durable. PostgreSQL also relies on the operating system's page cache, so a page can be cached twice, which is one reason its shared_buffers is usually set to a fraction of RAM rather than most of it.

cards.title: Worked example: 99.9% versus 99%
cards.body: A hit ratio that looks barely changed can mean ten times the storage reads.
steps: Assume queries touch 50,000 pages a second; a cached page costs about 0.001 ms and a storage read about 0.1 ms (illustrative SSD figures)
Hit ratio 99.9%: 0.1% of 50,000 = 50 storage reads a second
Hit ratio 99%: 1% of 50,000 = 500 storage reads a second, ten times as many
Hit ratio 90%: 10% of 50,000 = 5,000 storage reads a second, a hundred times as many
Average cost per page: about 0.0011 ms at 99.9%, 0.002 ms at 99% and 0.011 ms at 90%; latency follows the misses

cards.title: The working set
cards.body: The working set is the set of pages the current workload touches repeatedly: the upper levels of every index, recent orders, active users. It is usually much smaller than the database. A 2 TB database whose queries mostly touch the last week of data can run well with 64 GB of memory. When the working set grows past memory, because data grew, a new feature reads old history, or a new index competes for space, latency does not rise gently. Misses jump, every query waits on storage, and the slowdown seems to arrive overnight.

cards.title: Trap: one big scan evicting the hot pages
cards.body: With a plain least-recently-used cache, one report that scans a huge table would push every hot page out. Engines defend against this. PostgreSQL gives large sequential scans a small ring of buffers that they reuse, so they cannot flood shared_buffers. InnoDB inserts newly read pages at a midpoint of its list, so a page must be touched again before it joins the hot end. The defences are partial: scans still compete for the operating system cache and storage bandwidth. Run large reports on a replica, and watch the hit ratio when new batch jobs appear.

cards.title: Edge case: a cold cache after restart or failover
cards.body: After a restart the buffer pool is empty, and after a failover the promoted replica's cache holds whatever that replica was serving. For the first minutes, queries run at storage speed. By default InnoDB saves the list of its most recently used pages (25% of the buffer pool) at shutdown and reloads them at startup. PostgreSQL offers the pg_prewarm extension to load chosen tables or the previous cache contents. Include warm-up in failover tests, and size capacity so the system survives a few minutes of cold-cache latency.

cards.title: Misconception: “more memory always fixes it”
cards.body: Memory fixes misses caused by a working set that is slightly too big. It does not fix a query that reads far more pages than it needs, such as a missing index forcing a scan of 10 million pages for 10 rows. Check rows examined against rows returned, and pages read per query (for example EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) in PostgreSQL), before buying RAM. Often an index shrinks the working set more than a bigger server would.

questions.prompt: A database's buffer hit ratio fell from 99.9% to 99% after a feature launch, while pages requested per second stayed the same. What happened to storage reads?

choices.label: They rose by about 1%
They rose about tenfold
They stayed flat; only CPU time grew
They roughly doubled

questions.explanation: The miss rate went from 0.1% to 1%, ten times larger, and storage reads are requests × miss rate. A 1% rise confuses the change in hit ratio with the change in misses. Storage reads cannot stay flat when misses grow, and doubling would need a miss rate of 0.2%.

questions.prompt: Queries touch 80,000 pages a second at a 98% buffer hit ratio. How many storage reads a second is that?
assumptions: 98% hit ratio, so a 2% miss rate
questions.explanation: Sanity check: only misses reach storage. 78,400 is the number of hits, and 160 uses a 0.2% miss rate instead of 2%.

questions.prompt: A 3 TB store ran smoothly for a year on a server with 128 GB of memory. A new feature lets users browse their full purchase history, and latency jumps. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The data passed a hard size limit for one single server
Older rows have moved to a slower storage format on disk over the year
The working set outgrew memory, so many pages now come from storage
Index depth grew from 3 levels to about 30

questions.explanation: Old purchases that nobody looked at before are now part of the working set, so pages that were never cached are requested constantly. The data size did not change with the launch; the access pattern did. Old rows use the same storage format as new ones. B-tree depth grows logarithmically, so 3 TB is still only a few levels.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't one full scan of a huge table push every hot page out of a PostgreSQL or InnoDB cache?

choices.label: Scans read through the operating system cache and bypass the pool
Hot pages are pinned in memory until the server restarts
Scans reuse a small ring of buffers or enter the list mid-way
Scanned pages are compressed so they take little space

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL gives large sequential scans a small ring buffer, and InnoDB inserts new pages at the midpoint of its list, so a one-time scan cannot displace frequently used pages. Scans do go through the buffer pool. Pages are pinned only while a query is using them, not until restart. Pages are not compressed just because a scan read them.

questions.prompt: A query needs page 4711 of a table, and the buffer manager does not hold it. Sequence what the buffer manager does.

items.label: Load page 4711 from storage into that slot
Pick a victim slot with the clock sweep or LRU list
Pin the slot and hand the page to the query
Find no slot for page 4711 in the buffer mapping table
Flush the victim first if it holds unsaved changes

questions.explanation: A slot must be free before the new page can be read into it, and a dirty victim must be saved before its slot is reused, after its log records are flushed. Background writers try to keep clean pages available so queries rarely have to write before they can read.

approaches.label: Add more indexes on the orders table
approaches.description: Index tuning

approaches.label: Raise the connection pool size
approaches.description: More concurrency

approaches.label: Move to a 384 GB server now and partition or archive old orders
approaches.description: Memory plus a smaller hot set

rationaleOptions.label: More connections let storage serve misses faster
Memory larger than the working set turns most reads back into hits
Extra indexes shrink the working set
Moving old orders out stops the hot set from growing without limit

rationaleConflicts.r3: More concurrent queries waiting on storage only lengthen the storage queue.
rationaleConflicts.r4: New indexes add pages that compete for the same memory, unless they replace a scan with a far smaller lookup.

questions.explanation: Memory buys time: 184 GB of headroom at 5 GB a month lasts about three years. Partitioning or archiving old orders keeps the working set near the 90 days that matter, so the fix lasts.

mechanism.title: How a database decides which pages live in memory
steps: Tables and indexes are stored as fixed-size pages. Every read of a row or index entry is a request for a page, and the buffer pool is a fixed area of memory holding the pages used most recently, with a mapping table from page id to slot.

On a hit, the query pins the slot, reads the rows and unpins it, which takes microseconds. On a miss, the buffer manager picks a victim slot. If the victim is dirty, it is written out first, after its log records are on disk. The needed page is then read from storage, which takes around a tenth of a millisecond on SSD and milliseconds on network or spinning storage.

Victims are chosen by an approximation of least recently used: PostgreSQL uses a clock sweep with usage counts, InnoDB a list split into young and old parts. Both protect hot pages against one-off reads: PostgreSQL sends large scans through a small ring of buffers, and InnoDB inserts new pages at a midpoint so they must be touched again to become hot.

The working set is the part of the database that the workload keeps touching. While it fits, the miss rate is low and stable. When it stops fitting, every additional gigabyte of working set adds misses, and latency climbs quickly, because each miss costs about a hundred times a hit.

Below the buffer pool sits the operating system page cache. PostgreSQL reads through it, so a page missing from shared_buffers may still be in the OS cache and cost far less than a storage read; InnoDB is usually configured to bypass it with direct I/O and given most of the memory instead.

After a restart or failover the cache is empty or holds another server's pattern. Warm-up tools reload the pages that were cached before, and capacity plans should allow for a few minutes at storage speed.

useWhen: Latency rose without a change in query plans: check whether misses rose
Capacity planning: estimate the working set and keep memory comfortably above it
Before a failover drill: plan warm-up for the replica that will take over
When adding batch jobs or reports: watch whether they push hot pages out
avoidWhen: Do not judge health by the hit ratio alone; compare the miss count with what storage can serve
Do not add memory to fix a query that reads millions of pages for a handful of rows; fix the query
Do not give PostgreSQL's shared_buffers nearly all RAM; the operating system cache and queries need it too
Do not run large one-off scans on the primary at peak if a replica can take them

columns: Average cost per page (0.001 ms hit, 0.1 ms miss)

numbers.title: From hit ratio to storage load
assumptions: 0.001 ms per hit, 0.1 ms per miss
steps: Misses = requests × (1 − hit ratio): at 99%, 50,000 × 0.01 = 500 a second.
Average cost = hit ratio × 0.001 + miss rate × 0.1: at 99%, 0.00099 + 0.001 ≈ 0.002 ms.
At 90%: 0.0009 + 0.01 ≈ 0.011 ms per page, about ten times the 99.9% figure of 0.0011 ms.
A query reading 2,000 pages: about 2.2 ms at 99.9%, about 4 ms at 99% and about 22 ms at 90%.
numbers.result: Falling from 99.9% to 90% makes the same query about ten times slower, all of it spent waiting on misses.

india.title: PostgreSQL and MySQL buffer documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual describes shared_buffers and suggests starting at about 25% of memory on a dedicated server, noting that PostgreSQL also relies on the operating system cache. The MySQL manual explains that the InnoDB buffer pool uses a variation of least recently used with a midpoint insertion strategy, so pages read by scans enter the old sublist, and documents saving the buffer pool contents at shutdown and restoring them at startup, enabled by default.

pitfalls.say: Look at misses per second: ten times the misses at 99% versus 99.9%

interactive.title: Right after failover
interactive.prompt: The primary fails and a replica that served only nightly reports is promoted. Normal traffic switches to it at once. What happens in the first minutes?

choices.label: Latency is high until the hot pages are read back into its cache

choices.label: Performance is unchanged, because replicas share the primary's cache

title: Choosing Column Types: Money, Time and Text
objectives: Store money exactly: decimal precision and scale, or integer minor units, with a currency code
Tell instants apart from wall-clock times and store each correctly
Pick text types, encodings and collations that compare the way users expect

cards.title: A column type is the first constraint
cards.body: The type of a column decides which values can be stored, how they compare and sort, and how many bytes each row needs. A good type rejects nonsense at the door: a date column cannot hold 31 February, and an integer cannot hold "twelve". Smaller fixed-size types also fit more rows on each page, so scans and indexes read less. Three kinds of data cause most of the trouble: money, time and text.

cards.title: Worked example: what numeric(12,2) does with each value
cards.body: A decimal column is exact, but its precision and scale are rules the database applies to every value written to it.
steps: numeric(12,2) allows 12 significant digits, 2 of them after the point, so the largest value is 9,999,999,999.99
Inserting 1234.5 stores 1234.50 exactly: decimal digits need no binary approximation, unlike double precision
Inserting 10.005 stores 10.01: PostgreSQL rounds to the declared scale, half away from zero, with no error
Inserting 12,345,678,901.00 fails with "numeric field overflow": it needs 11 digits before the point, and only 10 fit
Integer minor units sidestep scale: ₹1,234.50 is 123450 paise, and a bigint holds about 9.2 × 10^16 rupees

cards.title: Instants and wall-clock times
cards.body: Most timestamps record an instant: when an order was paid. Store these as an instant, normally a timestamp with time zone, which PostgreSQL stores internally in UTC and converts to the session time zone on output; the zone the value was written with is not kept. A timestamp without time zone is only a wall-clock reading with no zone, so the same value means different instants in Delhi and New York. Future local events are different: "9:00 in Berlin on 3 June next year" should be stored as the local time plus the IANA zone name (Europe/Berlin), because zone rules can change before the date arrives. Engines differ here: MySQL TIMESTAMP converts from the session time zone to UTC and only reaches 2038-01-19, while DATETIME stores the value as written.

cards.title: Text: encoding, length and collation
cards.body: Use a Unicode encoding that covers every character, including emoji. In MySQL that means utf8mb4: the older utf8 name is an alias for utf8mb3, which stores at most 3 bytes per character and rejects 4-byte characters such as emoji. Length limits are business rules; in PostgreSQL, varchar(n) and text are stored the same way, so a limit costs nothing but should match a real rule. The collation decides sort order and equality. MySQL's default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is accent- and case-insensitive, so 'Jose' = 'José' and a unique index treats them as the same value; a binary or case-sensitive collation does not. It also decides what an index can do. In PostgreSQL, a B-tree index under a linguistic collation such as en_US cannot answer LIKE 'Ash%' as a range; an index built with text_pattern_ops, or a column in the C collation, can.

cards.title: Trap: local times stored without a zone
cards.body: An application writes the server's local time into a column without a zone. In America/New_York, clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00 on 1 November 2026, so 01:30 happens twice and a row stamped 01:30 matches two different instants. In spring, 02:30 never happens at all. Moving the server or changing its zone setting silently shifts the meaning of every old row. Store instants with a zone, or in UTC, and convert only for display.

cards.title: Edge case: currencies without two decimals
cards.body: Not every currency has 2 minor digits: ISO 4217 lists 0 for the Japanese yen and 3 for the Kuwaiti dinar and Bahraini dinar. Store the currency code next to every amount. Then either give the column a scale that covers every currency you accept, such as numeric(15,3), and validate decimals per currency, or store integer minor units and keep each currency's exponent in a lookup table. A numeric(14,2) column given 1.234 KWD silently stores 1.23.

questions.prompt: An order_total column is numeric(8,2). A ₹12,50,000.00 order (1.25 million rupees) fails to insert with "numeric field overflow". Why?

choices.label: Precision 8 with scale 2 leaves 6 digits before the point
numeric cannot store amounts above one million exactly
The value has more decimal places than the column allows
The Indian digit grouping in the amount confuses the parser

questions.explanation: numeric(8,2) holds 8 significant digits with 2 after the point, so its largest value is 999,999.99, and 1,250,000.00 needs 7 digits before the point. Widen it, for example to numeric(14,2). numeric is exact up to whatever precision you declare, far beyond a million. The value has exactly 2 decimals, and extra decimals are rounded, not rejected. The database receives a number, not a string with separators.

questions.prompt: An amount column stores paise in a 32-bit signed integer. What is the largest amount it can hold, in millions of rupees?
questions.explanation: Design implication: a busy merchant's yearly total passes ₹21 million, so totals and balances need a 64-bit integer or a decimal type. 2,147 forgets that the unit is paise, not rupees; 42.9 uses the unsigned range, which signed columns do not have.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL timestamptz column receives '2026-06-03 09:00 Europe/Berlin'. A session whose TimeZone is Asia/Kolkata reads it back. What does it see?
questions.explanation: timestamptz stores the instant, 07:00 UTC, and shows it in the reading session's zone: 12:30 in India. The name Europe/Berlin is not kept, so store it in its own column if you need it later. 09:00+02:00 is the same instant shown in Berlin time, which only a Berlin session would see. 09:00+05:30 keeps the wall-clock digits and changes the instant. 13:30 uses Berlin's winter offset of +01:00, but on 3 June Berlin is on summer time.

questions.prompt: A log table stores New York local time without a zone. Which row cannot be mapped to a single instant?

choices.label: 2026-11-01 01:30, the night clocks went back
2026-11-01 03:30, after the change
2026-07-04 12:00, a summer holiday
2026-12-31 23:59, the last minute of the year

questions.explanation: On 1 November 2026 New York clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 occurred twice, once in daylight time and once in standard time. 03:30 that day, noon in July and 23:59 on 31 December each occurred exactly once, so they map to one instant, as long as you know the zone.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL database uses the en_US.UTF-8 collation. WHERE name LIKE 'Ash%' ignores the B-tree index on name and scans the table. Why?

choices.label: Its sort order cannot serve a LIKE prefix as an index range
LIKE patterns do not use B-tree indexes at all in PostgreSQL
The index is rebuilt after inserts and is not ready yet
Prefix matches need a GIN index over the whole column

questions.explanation: Under a linguistic collation the planner cannot turn LIKE 'Ash%' into a range of index keys. An index created with text_pattern_ops, or a column in the C collation, can serve it. With such an index, or the C collation, a fixed-prefix LIKE does use a B-tree. B-tree indexes are maintained on every insert, not rebuilt later. A trigram GIN index can serve LIKE too, including infix patterns, but a prefix needs only the pattern-ops B-tree.

questions.prompt: Order how an app should handle a meeting time a user types in, from input to display.

items.label: Store the instant in a timestamp-with-zone column
Receive the local time and the user's zone name
Read it back and convert to each viewer's zone for display
Convert to an instant with the time zone database

questions.explanation: The zone name is needed to resolve the local time, conversion happens once on the way in, and every viewer sees the same instant in their own zone. This suits meetings that happen soon; for events far in the future, keep the local time and zone as entered and resolve the instant later.

questions.prompt: Users in India, Germany and the United States create orders. Finance wants daily totals by each user's local calendar day.
constraints: Daylight saving changes in two of the countries

approaches.label: Server-local timestamps
approaches.description: timestamp without zone, filled with the server's clock

approaches.label: Text timestamps
approaches.description: ISO strings with offsets, such as 2026-03-08T09:30:00+05:30

approaches.label: Instants plus zone names
approaches.description: timestamp with time zone, and each user's IANA zone for reports

rationaleOptions.label: Instants compare and sort correctly whatever zone they came from
ISO strings sort chronologically even with different offsets

Server-local times avoid conversions, so totals are simpler

rationaleConflicts.r3: Text sorts character by character, so 09:30+05:30 sorts after 08:00+00:00 although it is the earlier instant.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Server-local values have no zone, so the local day of a user elsewhere cannot be worked out reliably, and daylight saving repeats or skips hours.

flashcards.back: Decimal type or integer minor units, plus a currency code; never binary floating point
Timestamp with time zone (stored as UTC); convert only for display
