mechanism.title: What a column type decides
steps: The type fixes which values are legal. Inserting 31 February into a date column, or text into an integer column, fails before any application bug can spread it.
The type fixes how values compare. Numbers compare numerically, text compares by collation, and timestamps compare as points in time, which is why a number stored as text sorts 10 before 9.
The type fixes the size. An 8-byte timestamp is about a third of the 25-character text "2026-10-26T09:30:00+05:30", and the difference repeats in every row and every index entry.
Exactness depends on the type. Floating point trades exactness for range and speed, which suits measurements; decimal and integer types are exact, which money needs.
Time zone handling depends on the type. Instants should be stored with a zone or in UTC; wall-clock values without a zone need the zone stored beside them.

Changing a type later is costly. On a large table, converting a column usually rewrites every row and its indexes, and every reader must agree on the new meaning, so a few minutes spent choosing types at design time saves a migration later.

useWhen: Designing a new table: pick types for the rules the data must follow
Storing money: decimal or minor-unit integers, with a currency code
Storing event times: timestamp with time zone
Storing future appointments: local time plus zone name
avoidWhen: Do not store money in float or double columns
Do not store numbers or dates as text "for flexibility"
Do not pick varchar lengths at random; match a real rule or leave text unbounded
Do not rely on the server's time zone for meaning

rows: numeric(14,2) or bigint minor units, plus currency
timestamp without zone in server time
Unicode text (utf8mb4 in MySQL), chosen collation

numbers.title: What text timestamps cost
assumptions: ISO text with offset: 25 characters plus about 1 byte of length header
steps: Native type: 100,000,000 × 8 bytes = 0.8 GB.
Difference: about 1.8 GB in the table, and again in every index that includes the column.
The native type also sorts correctly and rejects impossible dates.
numbers.result: Native types save space and, more importantly, compare and validate correctly.

india.title: PostgreSQL numeric and date/time documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual describes numeric as especially recommended for monetary amounts and other quantities where exactness is required, and calls the floating-point types inexact. It also states that all time-zone-aware dates and times are stored internally in UTC and converted to local time in the zone set by the TimeZone parameter before being shown to the client.

pitfalls.trap: “Float is fine if we round on display”
pitfalls.say: Totals still drift; store decimal or minor units

pitfalls.trap: “We store UTC, so zones never matter”
pitfalls.say: Future local events and local-day reports still need the zone name

pitfalls.trap: “numeric(10,2) is big enough”
pitfalls.say: Precision limits digits before the point; size it for the largest total, not one price

takeaways: Money: exact types plus currency code and minor units
Instants: timestamp with time zone; future local times: local time plus zone name
Text: full Unicode, deliberate collation, limits that match real rules
Native types are smaller and compare correctly; text copies are neither

interactive.title: Too many decimals for the column
interactive.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a price column is numeric(12,2). An import inserts the value 10.005. What is stored?

choices.feedback: That would be truncation; PostgreSQL rounds to the declared scale instead.
Right: the value is rounded to 2 decimal places, half away from zero, with no error or warning.

choices.label: An error, because the value has 3 decimals
choices.feedback: Only too many digits before the point raise an error; extra decimals are rounded.

interactive.reveal: Scale is enforced by rounding, silently. If an extra decimal means bad input, reject it before it reaches the column: the value is rounded to the column type before any CHECK constraint sees it.

seeAlso.why: Types are one kind of constraint, alongside keys, NOT NULL and CHECK
Clocks, skew and ordering events across services
Choosing the type of the primary key itself
Money in application code: rounding rules, splitting amounts and currency
Time zones in business logic: schedules, daylight saving and local days
Text in a backend: Unicode normalisation, case folding and length limits

title: JSON Columns in a Relational Database
objectives: Decide which data belongs in a JSON column and which in real columns
Index JSON for the queries you run
Avoid type and rewrite surprises inside JSON values

cards.title: When a JSON column fits
cards.body: Relational databases can store JSON documents in a column and query inside them. This fits data whose shape varies by row and is read as a whole: product attributes that differ by category, user settings, or a webhook payload kept as received. It fits poorly for fields you join on, enforce rules on, aggregate in reports or update often. Those deserve real columns with types, constraints and foreign keys. A common design is a hybrid: typed columns for the core fields, plus one JSON column for the long tail.

cards.title: Worked example: a product catalogue with variable attributes
cards.body: Shoes have sizes and fabrics have widths, but every product has a price and a SKU.
steps: Real columns: id, sku (unique), price, category_id (foreign key), updated_at
JSON column attrs: {"brand": "Acme", "size": 9, "colour": "red"} for shoes, other keys for fabrics
Filter by any attribute: WHERE attrs @> '{"brand": "Acme"}', served by a GIN index on attrs
One key queried constantly: an expression index on (attrs->>'brand') or a generated column
Price stays a typed column, so reports and CHECK (price >= 0) work as usual

cards.title: json versus jsonb, and engine differences
cards.body: PostgreSQL has two types. json stores the text exactly as received, keeping whitespace, key order and duplicate keys, and reparses it on every use. jsonb stores a parsed binary form: it drops whitespace, does not keep key order, keeps only the last of duplicate keys, and supports GIN indexes. Use jsonb unless you need the original text. MySQL has one JSON type, stored in a binary format and validated on insert; it is indexed through generated columns, functional indexes or, for arrays, multi-valued indexes (8.0.17 and later).

cards.title: Indexing inside JSON
cards.body: Match the index to the query. A GIN index on a jsonb column serves containment (@>) and key-existence queries on any key; the jsonb_path_ops variant is smaller and faster but supports containment and path queries only. For equality or ranges on one key, a B-tree expression index on (attrs->>'brand') is smaller and also supports ORDER BY. A generated column that extracts the key gives it a real type, so it can be indexed, constrained and read by tools that do not understand JSON.

cards.title: Trap: comparing JSON numbers as text
cards.body: In PostgreSQL, ->> returns text. So WHERE data->>'qty' > '5' compares strings: '7' passes, but '12' fails, because '1' sorts before '5'. Cast the value, as in (data->>'qty')::int > 5, or compare jsonb to jsonb. The same applies to dates inside JSON, which are only strings until you cast them. Missing keys return NULL, so every reader must decide what an absent key means.

cards.title: Edge case: one small change rewrites the whole document
cards.body: In PostgreSQL, updating one key of a jsonb value writes a new copy of the whole value in a new row version, plus its log records. A 100 KB document whose counter changes 50 times a second rewrites about 5 MB a second before compression. MySQL 8.0 can update some JSON values in place with JSON_SET, JSON_REPLACE or JSON_REMOVE, but large rewrites are still common. Keep counters and fast-changing fields in their own columns or rows, and keep documents for data that changes rarely.

questions.prompt: An orders table is adding a JSON column. Which field is the best fit for it?

choices.label: customer_id, used to join to customers
The order total, summed in finance reports
Gift-wrap options that vary by shop
The status, which a CHECK rule restricts

questions.explanation: Optional, shop-specific details are read with the order and rarely queried on their own, which is what a document column suits. A join key needs a foreign key and a typed index. Totals used in reports need a numeric type. A status with allowed values needs a constraint, which a typed column gives you directly.

questions.prompt: A service must keep each webhook body unchanged so it can verify the sender's signature later. Which PostgreSQL type fits?

choices.label: jsonb, because it is the faster type
json or text, which keep the original text
jsonb with a GIN index on the body
A typed column for each field in the body

questions.explanation: A signature covers the exact bytes. json and text keep whitespace, key order and duplicates as received. jsonb normalises the document, so re-serialising it gives different bytes and the signature check fails; an index does not change that. Splitting into columns loses the original text too. A jsonb copy can sit alongside for querying.

questions.prompt: WHERE attrs @> '{"brand": "Acme"}' scans 5 million rows of a jsonb column. Which index serves it?

choices.label: A B-tree index on the whole attrs column
A hash index on attrs
A GIN index on attrs
An expression index on (attrs->>'colour')

questions.explanation: GIN indexes the keys and values inside each document, which is what containment needs. A B-tree or hash index on the whole value helps only when matching the entire document. An expression index on colour serves queries on colour, not brand.

questions.prompt: WHERE data->>'qty' > '5' returns orders with qty 7 but not qty 12. Why?

choices.label: ->> returns text, so the values compare as strings
JSON numbers above 9 are stored as floating point
The GIN index skips numbers with two digits
qty 12 rows were written before the index existed

questions.explanation: As text, '12' sorts before '5' because '1' < '5'. Cast with (data->>'qty')::int > 5. JSON numbers are not converted to floats at 10. GIN does not serve this text comparison at all, and an index never changes which rows match, only how they are found.

questions.prompt: A 100 KB jsonb document holds a counter that is updated 50 times a second, and each update rewrites the whole document. About how many GB a day are rewritten, before compression?
questions.formula: document size × updates per second × seconds per day
questions.explanation: Design implication: moving the counter to its own column or row cuts this to a few bytes per update. 5 is the per-second figure in MB, and 43.2 drops a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: Lookups filter on attrs->>'sku_ref' = $1 and then sort by that same key. Which index fits best?

choices.label: A GIN index on the whole attrs document
A B-tree expression index on (attrs->>'sku_ref')
A hash index on the attrs column as a whole
A block-range index on attrs, which stays very small

questions.explanation: An expression B-tree stores one extracted value per row, serves equality and can return rows in key order. GIN serves containment and key-existence across all keys, is larger, and cannot provide ordering. A hash index on the whole document matches only identical documents. Block-range indexes suit values that follow physical row order, which JSON keys rarely do.

questions.prompt: A payments service stores events from 12 payment providers. Each has its own fields, but every event has an amount, currency, status and merchant.

approaches.label: All JSON
approaches.description: One jsonb column per event, nothing else

approaches.label: Hybrid
approaches.description: Typed columns for amount, currency, status and merchant; jsonb for the rest

approaches.label: All columns
approaches.description: A column for every field any provider has ever sent

rationaleOptions.label: Typed shared fields get constraints, foreign keys and exact sums
Putting everything in JSON makes reports just as fast
New provider fields land in JSON without a migration
A column per field keeps the schema complete and simple

rationaleConflicts.r3: Hundreds of mostly-null columns and a migration for every new provider field are neither simple nor complete for long.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Reports must extract and cast every value from JSON, and nothing enforces types or allowed values on them.

questions.explanation: Give the fields you report and enforce on real columns, and let JSON absorb the parts that vary.

flashcards.back: Variable, read-together data; not join keys, totals or constrained fields
jsonb: parsed, indexable, normalised; json: original text, reparsed each use
Cast before numeric or date comparisons
Rewrites the whole document; keep hot fields in columns

mechanism.title: How a database stores and searches JSON
steps: On insert the document is validated. PostgreSQL json keeps the text; jsonb and MySQL JSON parse it into a binary form with keys and values that can be found without reparsing.
Path operators read inside the document: ->, ->> and #> in PostgreSQL, ->, ->> and JSON_EXTRACT in MySQL. Extracted values are JSON or text until cast.

Indexes work on what you extract or on the document as a whole. An expression index stores one extracted value per row, like any B-tree. A GIN index stores every key and value as separate entries pointing to the rows that contain them.
Large documents are compressed and stored out of line. Reading one key still loads the whole value, and changing one key usually writes a whole new copy.
Nothing checks the shape of the document unless you add rules: CHECK constraints on extracted values, JSON schema validation in MySQL, or checks in the application.

Statistics are thinner inside documents. The planner knows a lot about a typed column but little about a key buried in JSON, so estimates for filters on JSON keys are rougher; an expression index or a generated column gives the planner statistics on that key too.

useWhen: Attributes that vary by row and are read with it
Keeping an external payload as received
Prototyping a field before it earns a real column
Sparse optional settings
avoidWhen: Join keys and foreign keys
Fields in reports, sums and constraints
Counters and fields that change many times a second
Data that every query reads key by key

numbers.title: The cost of a hot counter inside a document
assumptions: Illustrative; before compression and log overhead
steps: Per second: 100,000 bytes × 50 = 5 MB.
Per day: 5 MB × 86,400 ≈ 432 GB written as new row versions.
Moved to an 8-byte column: 8 × 50 × 86,400 ≈ 35 MB a day of changed values, plus fixed per-row overhead.
Old versions must also be cleaned up, which adds more work for the larger design.
numbers.result: Hot fields belong outside large documents; the saving here is roughly ten-thousand-fold in changed bytes.

india.title: PostgreSQL JSON documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual explains that json stores an exact copy of the input text that processing functions must reparse, while jsonb is stored in a decomposed binary format that is slightly slower to input but significantly faster to process and supports indexing. It also notes that jsonb does not preserve whitespace, key order or duplicate keys, keeping the last value when keys repeat.

pitfalls.trap: Putting join keys in JSON
pitfalls.say: Promote them to typed columns with foreign keys

pitfalls.trap: Comparing ->> results without casting
pitfalls.say: Cast to the right type, or the comparison is textual

pitfalls.trap: A GIN index for a one-key equality lookup
pitfalls.say: An expression B-tree is smaller and supports ordering

takeaways: Hybrid design: typed columns for the core, JSON for what varies
jsonb for querying; json or text only to keep the original bytes
Index what you query: GIN for containment, expression indexes for one key
Cast extracted values, and keep fast-changing fields out of documents

interactive.title: Duplicate keys in jsonb
interactive.prompt: The text {"plan": "basic", "plan": "pro"} is inserted into a PostgreSQL jsonb column. What is read back?

choices.label: {"plan": "basic", "plan": "pro"}
choices.feedback: That is what json (not jsonb) would return, keeping the input text.

choices.label: {"plan": "basic"}
choices.feedback: jsonb keeps the last value for a repeated key, not the first.

choices.label: {"plan": "pro"}
choices.feedback: Right: jsonb keeps only the last value for a duplicate key.

interactive.reveal: jsonb normalises documents: duplicate keys collapse to the last one, whitespace and key order are not kept. If exact input matters, store it as json or text.

seeAlso.why: GIN and other inverted indexes, which jsonb containment queries use
Document databases, the NoSQL family built around JSON-like records
Evolving JSON payload schemas without breaking readers

title: Prepared Statements and Plan Caching
objectives: Explain what preparing a statement saves and what it changes
Recognise when a cached generic plan is wrong for some parameter values
Use prepared statements safely with poolers and schema changes

cards.title: Parse once, run many times
cards.body: Every SQL statement is parsed, checked against the catalog, planned and then executed. A prepared statement sends the SQL once with parameter markers, such as WHERE customer_id = $1, and later executions send only the values. That saves repeated parsing and, if the plan is reused, repeated planning. It also keeps values out of the SQL text, which is the main defence against SQL injection. Many drivers prepare statements for you; the behaviour below applies whether you prepare explicitly or not.

cards.title: Worked example: what planning costs at high query rates
cards.body: Planning is cheap per query but adds up when the same statements run thousands of times a second.
steps: Assume 20,000 queries a second and 0.2 ms of planning each (illustrative)
Planning time: 20,000 × 0.2 ms = 4,000 ms of CPU every second
That is about 4 CPU cores spent only on planning
With reused plans, planning drops to near zero for those statements
Execution time is unchanged; only the repeated parse and plan work is saved

cards.title: Generic plans and custom plans
cards.body: A custom plan is made for the actual values of one execution. A generic plan is made once for any values and reused. PostgreSQL makes custom plans for the first five executions of a prepared statement, then switches to the generic plan if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average custom plan. The plan_cache_mode setting (PostgreSQL 12 and later) can force either behaviour. SQL Server compiles a plan for the parameter values seen at first compilation, caches it, and reuses it for later values; this is called parameter sniffing.

cards.title: When one plan does not fit every value
cards.body: Skewed data breaks the one-plan assumption. If 0.1% of orders are cancelled and 90% are delivered, WHERE status = $1 wants an index lookup for 'cancelled' and a sequential scan for 'delivered'. A generic or first-sniffed plan picks one and is badly wrong for the other, so the same query is fast for some users and slow for others. Fixes include forcing custom plans or recompiling just that statement, separate statements for the rare and common cases, and, in SQL Server 2022, parameter-sensitive plan optimisation, which caches several plans for one statement.

cards.title: Trap: varying SQL text defeats the cache
cards.body: Plans are cached by statement text. Gluing values into the SQL makes every statement new, so nothing is reused and injection becomes possible. IN lists of varying length do the same quietly: IN ($1), IN ($1, $2) and so on are different statements. In PostgreSQL, = ANY($1) with an array parameter keeps one statement for any length. Identifiers such as a sort column cannot be parameters; choose them from a fixed allowlist in code.

cards.title: Edge case: poolers and schema changes
cards.body: A prepared statement lives on one server connection. Behind a pooler in transaction mode, the next transaction may run on another connection, where the statement does not exist; poolers either track statements per connection or need session mode. PgBouncer 1.21 and later tracks protocol-level prepared statements when max_prepared_statements is set, but not SQL PREPARE. Schema changes invalidate cached plans, which are replanned on next use. In PostgreSQL, a prepared SELECT * whose result columns change after an ALTER TABLE fails with "cached plan must not change result type" and has to be prepared again.

questions.prompt: An app runs the same lookup 5,000 times a second with different ids. What does preparing it save?

choices.label: Execution time for each index lookup
Network time for returning the rows
Repeated parsing, and planning if the plan is reused
Disk reads, because the prepared statement caches the rows it returns

questions.explanation: Preparing moves parse and analysis to once per connection, and a reused plan skips planning as well. The index lookup itself runs on every execution. Result rows still cross the network. Prepared statements cache plans, not data; the buffer pool caches pages either way.

questions.prompt: Planning takes 0.3 ms per statement, and a service sends 15,000 statements per second. How many processor cores does planning alone occupy?
assumptions: 1 core = 1,000 ms of CPU per second
questions.formula: queries per second × planning ms ÷ 1,000 ms per core
questions.explanation: Design implication: on a 16-core server that is over a quarter of the CPU, which plan reuse could give back to execution. 45 and 0.45 move the decimal point by one place in either direction.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL prepared query by status ran five times for 'delivered', which matches 90% of rows. From the sixth run, calls for 'cancelled' (0.1% of rows) are slow. What happened?

choices.label: Its statistics expired after five runs and were not rebuilt
It switched to a generic plan chosen for typical values
Its pages were evicted from the buffer pool
The connection reached a per-statement execution limit

questions.explanation: The first five runs got custom plans for a common value, so the generic plan, estimated for an average value, looked no costlier and was adopted. Rare values then get that one plan, which can read far more than they need. plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for that statement or session restores per-value planning. Had the first five runs been for rare values, their cheap custom plans would have kept the generic plan out. Statistics do not expire per run. Eviction would slow the first runs too. There is no limit on how often a statement may execute.

questions.prompt: In SQL Server, a procedure first ran for a customer with 2 million orders and cached a scan plan. Small customers are now slow. What fixes it at the source?

choices.label: Restart the server every night to clear the cache
Add memory so the large scan plan runs from cached pages instead
Recompile that statement per call, or plan for typical values
Rebuild every index on the orders table weekly

questions.explanation: The cached plan suits the first value it saw. A recompile hint on that statement, an OPTIMIZE FOR hint, or parameter-sensitive plan optimisation in SQL Server 2022 match the plan to the values. A restart only clears the cache until the next unlucky first call. More memory makes a wrong scan somewhat cheaper but still wrong. Rebuilding indexes may trigger recompiles by chance, not reliably.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a prepared statement on one connection.

items.label: Server parses and stores the statement
Server picks a custom or cached plan and executes
Client sends SQL with parameter markers to prepare
Rows go back and the statement stays for the next values
Client sends values for one execution

questions.explanation: Parsing happens once, at prepare time; each execution supplies values, chooses a plan and runs. The statement lives until the connection closes or it is deallocated.

questions.prompt: After adding a transaction-mode pooler, some requests fail with "prepared statement does not exist". Why?

choices.label: The pooler strips parameter markers from statements
The transaction ran on a different server connection
The database deletes prepared statements after each commit
Statements expire after a fixed number of seconds

questions.explanation: The statement was prepared on one server connection, and the next transaction was given another. Use a pooler that tracks prepared statements per connection, session mode, or unnamed per-execution statements. Poolers forward parameter markers unchanged. Prepared statements survive commits and have no time limit; they end with the connection or an explicit DEALLOCATE.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL report query filters by region with a parameter. One region holds 70% of rows; the other 40 regions are small. It runs about 50 times a minute, and planning takes 2 ms.

approaches.label: Force a generic plan
approaches.description: plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan for this query

approaches.label: Force custom plans
approaches.description: plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for this query

approaches.label: Inline the values
approaches.description: Build the SQL text with the region in it

rationaleOptions.label: Each run is planned for its own region, so small ones use the index
One generic plan suits every region equally well
At 50 runs a minute, 2 ms of planning is negligible
Inlining values is safe if quotes are escaped

rationaleConflicts.r3: The large region wants a scan and the small ones want an index; no single plan fits both.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Escaping is fragile and also makes every statement new text; parameters with custom plans keep safety and fit.

questions.explanation: Plan reuse pays off at thousands of executions a second. At 50 a minute, planning each run costs almost nothing and avoids the wrong plan.

flashcards.back: SQL sent once with parameter markers; later runs send only values
One plan for any value versus one plan per execution
SQL Server caches the plan for the first values it sees
May need custom plans, recompiles or separate statements

sources.title: SQL Server: Parameter sensitive plan optimization
OWASP: SQL injection prevention cheat sheet

mechanism.title: How a statement goes from text to a cached plan
steps: Parse: the SQL text becomes a tree, and names are resolved against the catalog. Preparing does this once and stores the result under a statement name on that connection.
Bind: each execution supplies parameter values. They are never parsed as SQL, so a value such as ' OR 1=1 -- is just a string.
Plan: the planner estimates costs with the statistics it has. For a custom plan it uses the actual values; for a generic plan it uses average selectivity.
Reuse: the engine decides whether to keep the generic plan. PostgreSQL compares its estimate with the custom plans so far; SQL Server reuses the first compiled plan until something invalidates it.
Invalidate: schema changes, new statistics or cache pressure throw plans away, and the next execution plans again.

Measure before tuning. Query statistics show how often each statement runs and its average time; if planning is a small share of that time, plan reuse is not where the gain is, and per-value plans are the safer default for skewed queries.

useWhen: High-rate, short queries where planning is a real share of the time
Every query that takes user input, for safety
Batch jobs that run one statement many times
Drivers and poolers that support prepared statements
avoidWhen: Do not force generic plans on queries over skewed columns
Do not build SQL text from values, even for speed
Do not rely on named prepared statements behind a pooler that does not track them
Do not leave IN lists of varying length when an array parameter exists

rows: Depends on the first value seen

numbers.title: When plan reuse matters
assumptions: Planning 0.2 ms, execution 0.3 ms per query
steps: Share of time in planning: 0.2 ÷ (0.2 + 0.3) = 40%.
At 10,000 queries a second, planning is 10,000 × 0.2 ms = 2 seconds of CPU per second, about 2 cores.
A report taking 2 s with 2 ms of planning: planning is 0.1% of the time.
A wrong plan that turns 2 s into 60 s costs far more than any planning it saved.
numbers.result: Reuse plans for fast, frequent queries; plan each time for slow or skewed ones.

india.title: PostgreSQL PREPARE documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual for PREPARE explains that a prepared statement can be executed with a generic plan or a custom plan, and that by default the first five executions use custom plans; a generic plan is then used if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average of the custom plans. It also documents plan_cache_mode for overriding this choice.

pitfalls.trap: “Prepared statements are always faster”
pitfalls.say: They save parsing and planning, but a generic plan can be far slower for skewed values

pitfalls.trap: Clearing the plan cache to fix a slow query
pitfalls.say: Fix why one plan does not fit: custom plans, recompiles or separate statements

pitfalls.trap: Named statements behind a transaction pooler
pitfalls.say: Use pooler support, session mode, or unnamed statements

takeaways: Preparing saves parse and plan work and keeps values out of SQL text
PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan after five custom ones; SQL Server reuses the first sniffed plan
Skewed data needs per-value plans for the affected statements
Keep statement text stable: array parameters, allowlisted identifiers

interactive.title: The sixth execution
interactive.prompt: A PostgreSQL prepared statement has run five times with custom plans, using default settings. What happens on the sixth execution?

choices.label: It always makes another custom plan
choices.feedback: Only if the generic plan looks clearly more expensive, or custom plans are forced.

choices.label: It may switch to a generic plan if its estimate is close enough
choices.feedback: Right: the generic plan is used if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average custom plan.

choices.label: The statement is deallocated and must be prepared again
choices.feedback: Prepared statements last until the connection closes or they are deallocated explicitly.

interactive.reveal: From the sixth run, PostgreSQL compares the generic plan's estimate with the custom plans so far. For skewed columns that comparison can pick a plan that is wrong for rare values.

title: Bulk Loading and Batched Writes
objectives: Explain where per-row overhead comes from in row-by-row writes
Choose bulk paths and batch sizes that load quickly and can resume
Handle indexes, constraints and retries during large loads

cards.title: Where the time goes in row-by-row writes
cards.body: Inserting one row per statement pays fixed costs every time: a network round trip, parsing, and, with autocommit, a commit that waits for the log to be flushed to disk. For a single row these costs dwarf the work of storing it. Batching shares them: many rows per statement, many statements per transaction, or a bulk-load command that streams rows. The aim is to spend time on storing data rather than on waiting.

cards.title: Worked example: one million rows, three ways
cards.body: Illustrative figures: 1 ms round trip, about 1 ms per commit flush.
steps: Row by row with autocommit: 1,000,000 round trips and commits, about 2 ms each, so roughly 2,000 s, over half an hour
Batches of 1,000 rows per statement and commit: 1,000 round trips and commits, about 2 s of waiting plus the insert work
Streaming bulk load (COPY in PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA in MySQL): one statement, rows streamed, parsed in bulk
Batch sizes beyond a few thousand give little more speed but larger transactions
The insert work itself, writing rows and index entries, stays the same in every case

cards.title: Bulk paths and batch sizes
cards.body: Engines provide fast paths for loading: COPY FROM in PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA in MySQL, BULK INSERT and bcp in SQL Server. Without them, multi-row INSERT … VALUES statements, or the driver's batch API, cut round trips. Batches of roughly hundreds to a few thousand rows usually capture most of the gain. Each batch should be its own transaction, so a failure loses one batch rather than the whole load, and the job should record the last key it committed so it can resume.

cards.title: Indexes, constraints and statistics during loads
cards.body: Every index adds work to every inserted row, and foreign keys and triggers add checks. For a new or empty table, load the data first and build the indexes afterwards, which is much faster than maintaining them row by row. For a live table, keep the indexes, because queries need them, and load in modest batches. After a large load, update statistics (ANALYZE in PostgreSQL) so the planner knows how big the table now is.

cards.title: Trap: one giant transaction
cards.body: Loading 50 million rows in one transaction looks tidy: all or nothing. But a failure near the end rolls everything back and starts over, the transaction holds its locks for the whole time, and replicas apply the change as one large burst, so they lag. In MVCC engines, a long transaction can also hold back the cleanup of dead rows across the database. Load in committed batches instead, into a staging table if the data must appear all at once, then switch over in one short step.

cards.title: Edge case: a retried batch inserts duplicates
cards.body: A batch commits, but the acknowledgement is lost to a timeout, so the job retries and inserts the same rows again. Give every incoming row a natural or idempotency key with a unique constraint, and insert with "do nothing on conflict" (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING in PostgreSQL, INSERT IGNORE or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE in MySQL). Alternatively, load into a staging table and merge from it, which also lets you validate rows before they touch the real table.

questions.prompt: A job inserts 2 million rows one per statement. The round trip to the database is 0.5 ms and everything else is ignored. About how many seconds does it spend on round trips?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 17 minutes of pure waiting. In batches of 1,000 rows it would be 2,000 round trips, about 1 s. 1,000,000 is the same total left in milliseconds, and 2,000 s uses a 1 ms round trip.

questions.prompt: Batching cut a load from 40 minutes to 3. Why not put all 5 million rows in one statement?

choices.label: Throughput keeps doubling with batch size, so one statement is fastest
Databases accept only 1,000 rows in any transaction
Gains flatten, while memory, lock time and the cost of a failure grow
Large statements skip the write-ahead log and risk losing data

questions.explanation: Once fixed costs are shared across a few thousand rows, larger batches add little speed but use more memory, hold locks longer and make a retry redo everything. Throughput does not keep doubling. Transactions have no general 1,000-row limit. Large statements are logged like small ones.

questions.prompt: A new empty table will receive 200 million rows and needs 5 indexes. What order is usually fastest?

choices.label: Create the indexes first so the load can use them
Load the rows, then build the indexes
Load half, build the indexes, load the rest
Load in random key order to spread the writes

questions.explanation: Building an index from complete data sorts once and writes pages sequentially; maintaining it during the load inserts entries one at a time into random places. Inserts do not use indexes to go faster. Building halfway only adds the slow path for the second half. Random order makes index maintenance worse, not better.

questions.prompt: A nightly job loads 30 million rows into a live table in one 3-hour transaction. What is the biggest risk?

choices.label: The database caps a transaction at 1 hour
A failure late in the run rolls everything back
Rows become visible to readers one at a time
Its rows are not written to the log until commit

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing means a failure at 2 h 50 min wastes the run and the retry may miss the window. Long transactions also hold locks, make replicas lag and delay cleanup. There is no general time cap. Readers see none of the rows until commit. Changes are logged as they are made, not only at commit.

questions.prompt: Order a staged import of a supplier file into a live products table.

items.label: Merge into products in batches, doing nothing on key conflicts
Stream the file into an empty staging table
Drop the staging table
Validate rows and remove duplicates in staging
Update the table statistics

questions.explanation: Staging takes the fast bulk path without touching live data, validation happens before anything reaches products, and batched merges keep transactions short. Statistics are refreshed once the data has landed, and staging is removed last.

questions.prompt: A batch times out, is retried, and the table ends up with two copies of 5,000 rows. What prevents this?

choices.label: A longer timeout on each batch so replies arrive in time
Fewer rows per batch
A unique key on the rows, with insert-if-absent
Retrying only when the database is idle

questions.explanation: The first attempt had committed; only the reply was lost. With a unique key and "do nothing on conflict", a retry inserts nothing it has already stored. Longer timeouts and smaller batches make lost replies rarer but cannot rule them out. Retry timing does not change whether the first attempt committed.

questions.prompt: Every night, 30 million rows from a partner must land in a live orders table before 06:00. The job sometimes fails halfway.

approaches.label: One transaction
approaches.description: Load everything, commit once at the end

approaches.label: Row by row
approaches.description: One autocommit insert per row

approaches.label: Committed batches
approaches.description: Batches of about 5,000 rows, each committed, with the last key recorded

rationaleOptions.label: Each batch commits, so a failure loses minutes of work, not hours
A single transaction is safest because it can be retried
Short transactions keep locks and replica lag small
Row-by-row inserts are easiest to resume

rationaleConflicts.r3: A retried single transaction repeats all of the work and may miss the window again.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Row-by-row inserts resume easily but pay a round trip and commit per row: hours for 30 million rows.

questions.explanation: Batches share the per-row costs, keep transactions short, and with a recorded key the job picks up where it stopped.

flashcards.back: Round trip, parse and commit flush; batching shares them
COPY (PostgreSQL), LOAD DATA (MySQL), BULK INSERT (SQL Server)
Load first, build indexes after, then update statistics
Unique key plus insert-if-absent, or staging and merge

mechanism.title: What happens to each row in a load
steps: The client sends the row, alone or in a batch. Each message pays a round trip, so the number of messages, not the number of rows, sets the network cost.
The server parses the statement and plans it. A bulk command or a multi-row statement does this once for many rows.
The row is written to a table page and one entry is added to each index. This is the real work, and it is the same however the rows arrive.
Constraints and triggers run: unique checks, foreign-key lookups, defaults. Each adds reads per row.
At commit, the log is flushed to disk. Committing every row pays one flush per row; committing every few thousand rows pays one per batch.

Afterwards, the planner still believes the old table size until statistics are refreshed, and replicas must replay every change. A load is finished when queries plan well against the new data and replicas have caught up, not when the last batch commits.

useWhen: Imports, backfills and migrations of more than a few thousand rows
Initial loads into new tables
Nightly partner or warehouse feeds
Event ingestion that can buffer for a moment
avoidWhen: Do not load millions of rows row by row with autocommit
Do not run a multi-hour load in one transaction on a live primary
Do not drop indexes on a live table that queries depend on
Do not retry batches without a unique key or a merge step

numbers.title: Choosing a batch size
assumptions: 1 ms round trip and commit wait per batch
0.02 ms of insert work per row
steps: Batch of 1: 1 + 0.02 = 1.02 ms per row.
Batch of 100: (1 + 100 × 0.02) ÷ 100 = 0.03 ms per row, about 34 times faster.
Batch of 10,000: (1 + 10,000 × 0.02) ÷ 10,000 = 0.0201 ms per row, barely better than 1,000.
numbers.result: Most of the gain arrives by a few hundred to a thousand rows; beyond that, larger batches only grow transactions.

india.title: PostgreSQL “Populating a database” guide
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual recommends turning off autocommit and doing all inserts in one transaction or a few, using COPY rather than INSERT, removing indexes and foreign-key constraints before loading a new table and recreating them afterwards, and running ANALYZE afterwards so the planner has up-to-date statistics. It also suggests raising maintenance_work_mem temporarily to speed up index creation, and notes that these steps matter most for one-time loads into new tables rather than routine inserts into live ones.

pitfalls.trap: “Bigger batches are always faster”
pitfalls.say: Gains flatten after a few thousand rows while risk keeps growing

pitfalls.trap: Dropping indexes on a live table to load faster
pitfalls.say: Only for new or offline tables; live queries need them

pitfalls.trap: Retrying after a timeout without a key
pitfalls.say: The first attempt may have committed; use insert-if-absent

takeaways: Per-row cost is mostly round trips and commits; batching shares them
Use bulk commands where possible, and batches of hundreds to thousands otherwise
New tables: load, then index, then analyse
Commit in batches, record progress, and make retries idempotent

interactive.title: Growing the batch size
interactive.prompt: A load uses batches of 1, then 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 rows. How does throughput change?

choices.label: It rises steeply at first, then flattens out
choices.feedback: Right: once fixed costs are shared across many rows, the per-row work dominates.

choices.label: It rises in proportion to the batch size every time
choices.feedback: Per-row insert work stays, so the speed-up cannot keep growing in proportion.

choices.label: It peaks at 10 rows and falls after that
choices.feedback: Batches of hundreds or thousands are usually much faster than 10.

interactive.reveal: Batching removes waiting, not work. When waiting is a small share of the time, larger batches mainly make transactions longer and failures costlier.

title: Using a Table as a Job Queue: SKIP LOCKED and Its Limits
objectives: Claim jobs from a table safely with several workers
Choose between holding a lock and taking a lease while a job runs
Recognise when a table queue should become a broker or a log

cards.title: Why use a table as a queue
cards.body: Many applications already have a relational database, and their background jobs are born inside a database transaction: "send the receipt for this order". Putting the job in a jobs table, in the same transaction as the order, means the job exists if and only if the order committed, with no second system to keep in step. A typical jobs table has an id, a status, a run_at time, an attempt count, a lease expiry and the job's payload.

cards.title: Worked example: two workers claim jobs without colliding
cards.body: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets each worker lock different rows instead of waiting for each other.
steps: Worker A: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' AND run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
A locks 10 rows. Worker B runs the same query, skips A's locked rows and gets the next 10
Without SKIP LOCKED, B would wait for A's locks; with a plain SELECT, both could take the same rows
Each worker sets status = 'running' and lease_until = now() + 5 minutes on its rows, then commits, so row locks last milliseconds
After the work, the worker deletes the job or marks it done; if it crashes, the lease expires and another worker can claim it

cards.title: Hold the lock, or take a lease
cards.body: One style keeps the transaction open while the job runs, holding the row lock. It is simple, and a crash releases the lock, so the job becomes available again. But each running job holds a connection and an open transaction for its whole duration, which in MVCC engines also holds back cleanup. The other style commits a claim with a lease expiry and works outside any transaction. It suits jobs longer than a second or two, but needs the claim query to take back expired leases and the finishing step to check that the worker still owns the job. SKIP LOCKED is available in PostgreSQL 9.5 and later, MySQL 8.0 and Oracle; SQL Server offers the READPAST hint for a similar effect.

cards.title: Indexes and churn
cards.body: A queue table is small but very busy: every job is inserted, updated at least once and then deleted. A partial index such as ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'ready' keeps the claim query reading only ready jobs. In PostgreSQL each update and delete leaves a dead row version, so vacuum must keep pace. A long-running transaction anywhere in the database stops that cleanup, dead entries pile up in the queue index, and claim queries that used to take a millisecond start scanning thousands of dead entries.

cards.title: Trap: read first, then update
cards.body: A worker runs SELECT … WHERE status = 'ready' LIMIT 1, then UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running' WHERE id = 42. Two workers can read job 42 in the same instant, both update it, and both run it. Make the claim one atomic step: lock with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside the claiming statement, or use a conditional UPDATE … WHERE id = 42 AND status = 'ready' and treat zero affected rows as "someone else got it". Even then, jobs can run twice after a lease expires, so job handlers must be idempotent.

cards.title: Edge case: when a table queue reaches its limits
cards.body: Each job costs several writes on the primary: insert, claim and delete, each with index updates and log records. Thousands of jobs a second compete with the application's own writes and keep vacuum busy. A table queue also hands each job to one worker and then forgets it. If many independent consumers must each read every event, or events must be replayed later, or ordering per key matters at high volume, a log such as Kafka or a dedicated broker fits better, often fed from the database through an outbox.

questions.prompt: Two workers sometimes run the same job. Each reads a ready job with a plain SELECT, then updates its status. What is the cause?

choices.label: Both read the row before either update committed
The jobs table lacks a primary key on id
The workers use different isolation levels
The status index is out of date until vacuum runs

questions.explanation: A plain SELECT takes no lock, so both see job 42 as ready and both update it. Claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional update that checks the status. A primary key does not stop two updates of the same row. Isolation levels differing does not create the race; it exists at Read Committed for both. Index maintenance is not deferred to vacuum.

questions.prompt: Worker A has locked 10 ready jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Worker B runs the same query. What does B get?

choices.label: B waits until A commits, then gets the same 10
B gets an error saying the rows are locked
B gets the next 10 unlocked ready jobs
B gets A's 10 rows, but as read-only copies

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED leaves out rows that cannot be locked immediately, so B moves on to other ready jobs at once. Waiting is the behaviour without SKIP LOCKED; an error is what NOWAIT does. Locked rows are not returned in any form.

questions.prompt: In a lease design, a worker crashes 2 minutes into a job whose lease lasts 5 minutes. What happens to the job?

choices.label: It is rolled back and becomes ready again at once for any worker
It stays running until the lease expires, then can be reclaimed
It is lost for good unless an operator resets its status by hand
The database restarts it on another worker

questions.explanation: The claim was committed, so nothing rolls back. After lease_until passes, the claim query treats it as available. Immediate release happens only in the hold-the-lock style, where the crash ends the transaction. The lease exists precisely so the job is not lost. Databases do not run jobs.

questions.prompt: A queue processes 2,000 jobs a second. Each job is inserted, updated once when claimed, and deleted when done. About how many million row writes a day does that add?
assumptions: 3 row writes per job: insert, claim, delete
questions.formula: jobs per second × writes per job × seconds per day
questions.explanation: Design implication: each of those writes also updates indexes and the log, and in PostgreSQL leaves dead versions for vacuum, so the queue can rival the application's own write load. 172.8 counts only the inserts, and 6 is the per-second figure in thousands.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a job in a lease-based table queue.

items.label: Do the work outside any transaction
Insert the job in the same transaction as the order
Delete the job only if this worker still holds the lease
Claim it with SKIP LOCKED and set a lease expiry
Commit the claim so the row lock is released

questions.explanation: The job is born with the business change, claimed atomically, and committed quickly; the work happens without an open transaction, and the final step checks ownership so a worker whose lease expired does not delete someone else's claim.

questions.prompt: Which new requirement is the clearest sign to move from a jobs table to a log or broker?

choices.label: Jobs must be created atomically with the order
Five services must each read every order event, and replay it
About 50 jobs a second must now be processed by the workers
Failed jobs should be retried three times before giving up

questions.explanation: Many independent consumers reading the same events, with replay, is what logs are built for; a jobs table hands each job to one worker and deletes it. Atomic creation is the main strength of a table queue. 50 jobs a second is modest for a table. Retries are a column and a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: An online shop on one PostgreSQL primary sends about 200 emails a minute after orders commit. No email may be sent for an order that rolled back.

approaches.label: Broker publish
approaches.description: Commit the order, then publish to a message broker

approaches.label: Jobs table
approaches.description: Insert a job in the order transaction; workers claim with SKIP LOCKED

approaches.label: Polling orders
approaches.description: Workers scan all orders every minute for unsent emails

rationaleOptions.label: The job commits or rolls back with the order
Publishing after commit is atomic with the order
SKIP LOCKED lets several workers share the queue without collisions
Scanning all orders each minute stays cheap as the shop grows

rationaleConflicts.r3: If the process dies between commit and publish, the email is never sent; a broker needs an outbox to be atomic.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A full scan grows with every order ever placed, while the work per minute stays the same.

questions.explanation: At a few emails a second a jobs table is ample, and it gives atomicity for free. Revisit it when volume or fan-out grows.

flashcards.back: Jobs commit or roll back with the business change
Lock rows you can get now, skip the rest; workers never collide
Committed claim with an expiry; expired leases are reclaimed
High churn, fan-out to many consumers, replay: use a log or broker

mechanism.title: How workers share a jobs table
steps: A producer inserts a row with status ready and a run_at time, inside the same transaction as the change that caused it. If that transaction rolls back, the job never existed.

A worker runs a claim query: ready rows due now, in run_at order, a small LIMIT, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. The engine walks the index, tries to lock each row, and skips any row another transaction holds.
The worker marks its rows running with a lease expiry and commits. Its locks are released within milliseconds, so other workers are never blocked for the length of a job.
The worker does the job, then deletes the row or marks it done, checking that it still owns the lease. On failure it increments attempts and sets a later run_at, a simple form of backoff.
The claim query also picks up running rows whose lease has expired, which is how work from crashed workers is recovered. Because that can run a job twice, handlers must be idempotent.

Cleanup keeps the table healthy. Done rows are deleted or moved to a history table, vacuum reclaims dead versions, and the partial index on ready jobs stays small as long as nothing holds back that cleanup for long.

useWhen: Jobs created by database transactions
Tens to a few hundred jobs a second
Teams that want one fewer system to run
Delayed jobs with a run_at time
avoidWhen: Thousands of jobs a second on a busy primary
Many consumers that each need every event
Replaying old events
Strict ordering per key at high volume

rows: No, can lose jobs on crash
Outbox table relayed to a broker
Yes, via the broker or log

numbers.title: What a table queue costs the primary
assumptions: Insert, claim update and delete per job
Two indexes on the jobs table
steps: Row writes: 500 × 3 = 1,500 a second.
Index writes: each insert adds 2 index entries and, when the claim changes an indexed column, the update adds more; roughly 1,500 to 3,000 a second.
Dead row versions left for vacuum: 500 × 2 = 1,000 a second, 86.4 million a day.
At 5,000 jobs a second all of this is ten times larger, which is where a broker starts to pay for itself.
numbers.result: A table queue is cheap at hundreds of jobs a second and an increasingly heavy tenant on the primary beyond that.

india.title: PostgreSQL SELECT documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual explains that with SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. It warns that skipping locked rows gives an inconsistent view of the data, so the option is not suitable for general-purpose work, but notes that it can be used to avoid lock contention when multiple consumers access a queue-like table.

pitfalls.trap: Claiming with a plain SELECT, then UPDATE
pitfalls.say: Claim atomically with SKIP LOCKED or a conditional update

pitfalls.trap: Holding a transaction open for a 10-minute job
pitfalls.say: Commit a lease and work outside the transaction

pitfalls.trap: Letting done rows accumulate
pitfalls.say: Delete or archive them, and watch vacuum on the queue table

takeaways: A jobs table gives atomic enqueue with the business change
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets workers claim different rows without waiting
Leases recover crashed work; handlers must be idempotent
Move to a broker or log for high churn, fan-out or replay

interactive.title: One job, two workers
interactive.prompt: Only one job is ready. Worker A has claimed it with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and has not committed yet. Worker B runs the same claim query. What happens?

choices.label: B waits for A to commit, then gets nothing
choices.feedback: SKIP LOCKED never waits for row locks; that is the point of it.

choices.label: B gets no rows, immediately
choices.feedback: Right: the only ready row is locked, so it is skipped and B sees an empty result at once.

choices.label: B gets the same job and both run it
choices.feedback: B cannot lock a row A holds, and SKIP LOCKED leaves it out.

interactive.reveal: Empty results are normal for a queue worker: it sleeps briefly or waits for a notification, then asks again.

title: Finding Slow Queries: Statement Statistics and Slow Logs
objectives: Rank queries by total load rather than by single slow runs
Read statement statistics to tell a bad plan from too much work
Go from a statement fingerprint to a verified fix

cards.title: Two views of query load
cards.body: Statement statistics group executions of the same query shape and keep running totals: calls, total and mean time, rows and pages read. PostgreSQL has the pg_stat_statements extension, MySQL the performance_schema statement digest tables, and SQL Server the Query Store. A slow query log records individual executions above a time threshold, with their actual text: log_min_duration_statement in PostgreSQL, slow_query_log with long_query_time in MySQL. Statistics show where the load is; the log shows concrete examples to investigate.

cards.title: Worked example: the slowest query is not the biggest problem
cards.body: Rank by total time, which is calls × mean time, because that is what the server spends.
steps: Query A: a monthly report, mean 2 s, 100 calls an hour: 200 s an hour
Query B: a product lookup, mean 5 ms, 200,000 calls an hour: 1,000 s an hour
B uses five times the server time of A, though each call is 400 times faster
Cutting B to 1 ms saves 800 s an hour; making A instant saves at most 200 s
Sort by mean time to find what annoys one user; sort by total time to find what loads the server

cards.title: Reading a statistics row
cards.body: Each row describes one normalised statement, with constants replaced by parameters. Look at rows per call: a high number suggests missing filters or pagination. Compare pages read from storage with pages found in cache: many reads point to a missing index or a working set larger than memory. In MySQL, rows examined against rows sent shows how much was read to produce the answer; 2,000,000 examined for 20 sent is a scan doing an index's job. Mean time hides outliers, so check the maximum or the standard deviation as well.

cards.title: From fingerprint to fix
cards.body: Take the top statements by total time. Get a real example with real values from the slow log or the application, run it under EXPLAIN with actual timings and buffer counts, and compare estimated rows with actual rows at each step. Fix the cause: an index, a rewrite, fresher statistics, or less work requested. Then compare the statement's statistics over the same length of time before and after. PostgreSQL's auto_explain module can log the plans of statements slower than a threshold, which helps when a plan changes only sometimes.

cards.title: Trap: the slow log shows only slow queries
cards.body: With long_query_time or log_min_duration_statement at 1 second, a server can run at 90% CPU and log nothing, because the load comes from millions of 5 ms queries. Logging every statement on a busy server is not the answer either: it adds I/O and can slow the database. Use statement statistics for the overall picture, keep the slow-log threshold for outliers, and sample if you need full text for fast queries.

cards.title: Edge case: fast on average, slow sometimes
cards.body: A statement averages 3 ms but users report occasional 4-second waits. Statistics that include the maximum or the deviation show it; the plan usually does not. Common causes are waiting for a lock held by another transaction, a cache miss after a restart or failover, and a plan that changes for some parameter values. Check wait events and lock waits for the slow moments (pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL, performance_schema in MySQL), not only the plan.

questions.prompt: A statement has a mean time of 40 ms and runs 50,000 times an hour. How many seconds of server time does it use per hour?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 2,000 s of work in a 3,600 s hour means this statement alone keeps more than half a core busy on average. 200 and 20,000 slip the decimal point by one place.

questions.prompt: Which statement should you tune first to reduce database load?

choices.label: Mean 8 s, 30 calls a day
Mean 12 ms, 400,000 calls a day
Mean 900 ms, 200 calls a day
Mean 1 ms, 100,000 calls a day

questions.explanation: Totals: 30 × 8 s = 240 s; 400,000 × 12 ms = 4,800 s; 200 × 0.9 s = 180 s; 100,000 × 1 ms = 100 s. The 12 ms statement carries twenty times the load of the 8-second one. Slow single runs matter for those users, but they are not where the server spends its time.

questions.prompt: CPU sits at 90%, but the slow log, set to 1 second, has been empty all day. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: The slow log is broken and needs a restart
The load comes from many queries under 1 second
CPU is used by the log writer itself
Queries only count as slow while waiting on disk

questions.explanation: Millions of fast statements can saturate a server without any single one crossing the threshold; statement statistics would show them. An empty log at a 1 s threshold is normal. Writing an empty log costs nothing. Time in the log is wall time, whether spent on CPU, disk or locks.

questions.prompt: A MySQL slow log entry shows rows_examined 2,000,000 and rows_sent 20. What does that suggest?

choices.label: The result was too large to send quickly
A filter is not served by an index
The network dropped most of the rows
The query cache returned old rows

questions.explanation: Reading two million rows to return 20 is a scan where an index lookup should be; check the plan and the filter columns. 20 rows is a small result. Rows sent counts what the server produced, not what arrived. MySQL 8.0 removed the query cache.

questions.prompt: Order a query-tuning pass.

items.label: Run EXPLAIN with actual timings and buffers
Compare statistics over an equal window afterwards
Sort statement statistics by total time
Fix the cause: index, rewrite or statistics
Get a real example with its actual values

questions.explanation: Pick by load, examine a concrete execution, change one thing, and confirm with the same measurement you started from. Run EXPLAIN with actual execution on writes only inside a transaction you roll back, or on a copy.

questions.prompt: A lookup averages 3 ms, yet users sometimes wait 4 seconds for it. Its plan looks fine. What should you check next?

choices.label: Whether the query needs a covering index
Lock waits and wait events at the slow moments
Whether the table should be partitioned
Whether the mean includes the planning time

questions.explanation: A good plan with rare long waits usually means the statement waited for something: a row lock, a cold cache, or a connection. Wait events and lock views show which. A covering index or partitioning changes typical speed, not rare 4-second stalls. Whether planning is counted cannot turn 3 ms into 4 s.

questions.prompt: A team wants production query monitoring on a primary that serves 20,000 statements a second.
constraints: See where total load comes from

approaches.label: Log every statement
approaches.description: Set the slow-log threshold to zero

approaches.label: Statistics plus a threshold
approaches.description: Statement statistics, a slow log at about 500 ms, sampled plan logging

approaches.label: Ad hoc only
approaches.description: Run EXPLAIN when someone complains

rationaleOptions.label: Aggregated statistics show total load per statement at low cost
Logging every statement has no measurable overhead
A threshold log captures the text and values of outliers
Complaints reliably point to the statements causing load

rationaleConflicts.r3: At 20,000 statements a second, full logging writes a large stream of text and can slow the server itself.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Users notice slow pages, not the fast queries that together use most of the server.

questions.explanation: Aggregate everything cheaply, log only what is slow, and add plans for the outliers.

flashcards.back: calls × mean time; rank by it to reduce load
Normalised queries with running totals: calls, time, rows, pages
Individual executions over a threshold, with real values
A large ratio means reading far more than you return

mechanism.title: How statement statistics are collected
steps: When a statement finishes, the engine computes a fingerprint of its normalised text, with literal values replaced by parameters, so WHERE id = 7 and WHERE id = 9 count as one statement.
It adds the execution's numbers to that statement's running totals: one more call, the elapsed time, rows returned, pages found in cache and pages read from storage.

Totals live in shared memory with a fixed number of entries. When there are more distinct statements than entries, the least-used are discarded, which is another reason to avoid statements whose text varies.
Totals grow from the last reset. To compare before and after a fix, take a snapshot, wait an equal period, and subtract, or reset at a known time.
Separately, the slow log writes one entry per execution above the threshold, with the full text and values, and in MySQL rows examined and sent.
Neither source shows why a statement waited. Lock views and wait-event sampling fill that gap and should be read alongside them when times vary widely.

Managed services and monitoring tools usually read these same views on a schedule and chart the differences, so the numbers on a dashboard are deltas of the totals described here, not a separate measurement.

useWhen: Before any tuning work, to choose what to tune
After a release, to spot statements whose cost rose
Capacity planning, to see which statements grow with traffic
Incident reviews, to find the statement behind a spike
avoidWhen: Do not tune by mean time alone
Do not log every statement on a busy primary
Do not compare totals over windows of different length
Do not trust a plan from EXPLAIN without actual timings

rows: Total load per statement, rows, pages
Real text and values of slow runs
Where one execution spent its time
What a session is waiting for now

numbers.title: Ranking by load
assumptions: Three statements from one hour of statistics
steps: Search: 120,000 calls × 15 ms = 1,800 s.
Checkout: 8,000 calls × 60 ms = 480 s.
Export: 12 calls × 30 s = 360 s.
Halving search saves 900 s an hour, more than removing the other two entirely.
numbers.result: The statement to tune first is the one with the largest calls × mean, which is often a fast one.

india.title: PostgreSQL pg_stat_statements documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual describes pg_stat_statements as a module that tracks planning and execution statistics of all SQL statements executed by a server. It explains that statements are combined into one entry when they have the same query structure, with constants replaced by parameter symbols, and lists columns such as calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, rows, and shared blocks hit and read.

pitfalls.say: Rank by total time to cut load

pitfalls.trap: Setting the slow log to zero in production

interactive.title: Two lookups, one entry?

choices.label: As two entries, one per id value

choices.label: As one entry with calls = 2
choices.feedback: Right: both normalise to WHERE id = $1 and share one row of totals.
