title: Estimating Table and Index Size
objectives: Estimate bytes per row, including the engine's per-row overhead
Estimate index size from entry width and how full pages are
Turn table size into disk, memory and recovery-time plans

cards.title: Why estimate size before you have the data
cards.body: Size drives several decisions at once: whether the working set fits in memory, how much disk to provision, and how long a backup restore, a replica rebuild or a full-table migration will take. A rough estimate made from the schema and expected row counts is usually within a factor of two, which is enough to tell a 50 GB table from a 5 TB one. The method is the same everywhere: bytes per row, rows per page, pages per table, then the same for each index.

cards.title: Worked example: 500 million orders in PostgreSQL
cards.body: Illustrative schema: id bigint, customer_id bigint, created_at timestamptz, total numeric, status smallint, plus a short note.
steps: Column data: about 70 bytes per row on average, including the variable-length total and note
Per-row overhead: a 23-byte tuple header padded to 24, plus a 4-byte line pointer in the page, so about 28 bytes
Per row: about 100 bytes, so 500,000,000 × 100 bytes ≈ 50 GB for the table
Primary key index on a bigint: about 20 bytes per entry, with leaf pages about 90% full, so 500,000,000 × 20 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 11 GB
Two more indexes of similar width: about 33 GB of indexes in total, two-thirds the size of the table

cards.title: Where the overhead comes from
cards.body: Every engine adds bytes to each row. In PostgreSQL the tuple header is 23 bytes and each row also has a 4-byte line pointer; values are aligned, so a boolean followed by a bigint wastes 7 bytes of padding, and ordering columns from widest to narrowest avoids it. A NULL takes a bit in a null bitmap, not the column's width. InnoDB stores each row in the clustered primary-key index with a 5-byte record header and two hidden fields, a 6-byte transaction id and a 7-byte roll pointer, and every secondary index entry carries the primary key. Pages are 8 KB by default in PostgreSQL and 16 KB in InnoDB, each with its own header.

cards.title: Indexes and how full their pages are
cards.body: An index entry holds the key, a pointer to the row and a small header. For an 8-byte key in PostgreSQL that is about 20 bytes, including the line pointer. How full the pages are matters as much as entry width. Keys that always arrive in increasing order fill leaf pages up to the fill factor, 90% by default for PostgreSQL B-trees. Random inserts split pages, which then sit about two-thirds to three-quarters full on average, so the same index can be a third larger. Updates and deletes leave further free space until it is reused or the index is rebuilt.

cards.title: Trap: counting only the column bytes
cards.body: Adding up column widths gives the smallest number you will ever see. Per-row overhead often adds 20 to 40% for narrow rows; indexes commonly add half the table size or more; free space and dead rows add more. Then the database is copied: a primary with two replicas holds three copies, backups add more, and the write-ahead log and temporary files need room. A disk plan built from raw column bytes can be short by a factor of five or more.

cards.title: Edge case: measure a sample instead of trusting the formula
cards.body: Variable-length values, compression and fill patterns are hard to predict. Load a representative sample, say a million realistic rows, build the planned indexes, and measure. In PostgreSQL, pg_relation_size, pg_indexes_size and pg_total_relation_size report the sizes; in MySQL, information_schema.TABLES reports data_length and index_length. Scale the measurement by the expected row count; if your formula and the sample differ by more than about 30%, trust the sample and find out why.

questions.prompt: A table will hold 200 million rows with about 92 bytes of column data each, plus 28 bytes of per-row overhead. About how many GB will the table take, before indexes?
assumptions: 92 bytes of data + 28 bytes overhead per row
Ignore page headers and free space
questions.explanation: Sanity check: overhead alone is 200 million × 28 bytes = 5.6 GB, nearly a quarter of the total. 18.4 forgets the overhead, and 2.4 drops a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: An index has 300 million entries of about 20 bytes each, and its leaf pages are about 90% full. About how many GB does it take?
questions.formula: entries × bytes per entry ÷ fill fraction
questions.explanation: Design implication: with random inserts the pages would be nearer 70% full, about 8.6 GB, so the insert pattern matters as much as the key width. 6 ignores the free space in each page, and 5.4 multiplies by 0.9 instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table's columns are, in order: is_active boolean, id bigint, is_deleted boolean, created_at timestamptz. How can it be made smaller?

choices.label: Change both booleans to smallint so they align better
Put the 8-byte columns first, then the booleans
Store created_at as text instead
Set the table fill factor to 100 so pages are packed full

questions.explanation: Each 8-byte value must start on an 8-byte boundary, so a boolean before it wastes 7 bytes of padding, twice here: the data takes 32 bytes instead of 18. The whole row is then padded to a multiple of 8, so with the 23-byte header each row shrinks from 56 to 48 bytes. smallint is wider than boolean and still needs padding. Text timestamps are larger. 100 is already the default table fill factor.

questions.prompt: An index built fresh last year is now 40% larger, though the table's row count barely changed. Keys are random UUIDs. What explains it?

choices.label: B-tree depth grows with the age of the index
Each entry gains a timestamp as it ages
Page splits from random inserts left pages partly empty
The index now stores every old row version forever

questions.explanation: A fresh build packs pages to the fill factor. Random inserts since then split full pages into half-empty ones, and deletes leave gaps, so the average page holds fewer entries. A rebuild packs them again. Depth grows with the number of entries, not age. Entries do not gain timestamps. Dead entries are cleaned up over time rather than kept forever.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a storage estimate for a new table.

items.label: Add per-row overhead and alignment padding
Add each planned index the same way
List the columns and their average widths
Multiply for replicas and add headroom for growth and logs
Multiply by rows, allowing for page fill

questions.explanation: Each step builds on the one before: row width, then rows, then indexes on top of the table, and only then the copies and headroom that turn database size into disk to buy.

questions.prompt: Tables and indexes total 400 GB on the primary. There are two replicas, and you want 30% headroom on each server. How much disk is needed across the three?

choices.label: About 520 GB
About 1,200 GB
About 1,560 GB
About 1,800 GB

questions.explanation: 400 GB × 1.3 = 520 GB per server, and three servers need 1,560 GB. 520 GB covers only the primary. 1,200 GB has three copies but no headroom. 1,800 GB adds 50% headroom rather than 30%. Backups are stored separately on top of this.

questions.prompt: A team must order disks for a new service. The schema is designed, but no production data exists, and the estimate must be within about 30%.

approaches.label: Column-width sum
approaches.description: Add the column widths and multiply by rows

approaches.label: Copy a similar system
approaches.description: Use the size of another team's database

approaches.label: Formula checked by a sample
approaches.description: Estimate with overhead and indexes, then load a realistic sample and measure

rationaleOptions.label: The formula covers overhead, page fill and every index
Column widths alone come within 30% for most tables
A measured sample catches compression and variable widths the formula misses
Another system's size transfers well because databases are similar

rationaleConflicts.r3: Raw column bytes leave out row overhead, indexes and free space, which together can double the size.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Row counts, widths and indexes differ between systems, so their sizes do not transfer.

questions.explanation: A formula gives the structure of the answer and a sample checks it; together they are reliable enough to buy hardware.

flashcards.back: Column data + per-row header + line pointer + padding
entries × entry width ÷ page fill fraction
Sequential inserts pack pages; random inserts leave them about 70% full
Tables + indexes, × copies, + headroom, then measure a sample

mechanism.title: How rows and index entries fill pages
steps: Storage is divided into fixed pages: 8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB. Each page has a header, then rows or index entries, then free space.

Each row carries a header with visibility and layout information. In PostgreSQL that is 23 bytes plus a 4-byte pointer from the page's item array; InnoDB uses a record header plus hidden transaction fields.

Values are stored in column order and aligned to their natural boundaries, so the order of columns changes how much padding a row needs. NULLs cost a bit, and long values may be compressed or moved out of line.
Index entries hold the key and a row pointer (PostgreSQL) or the primary key (InnoDB secondary indexes). They are packed into leaf pages up to a fill factor and split when full.
The table and its indexes grow with inserts and with dead versions left by updates and deletes until cleanup reuses the space. Rebuilding packs pages again.
Estimates therefore come in layers: raw data, then overhead, then page fill, then indexes, then copies. Each layer is simple, and missing any one of them is the usual source of large errors.

useWhen: Choosing server memory and disk
Predicting restore and replica rebuild times
Deciding whether to partition or archive
Comparing schema options, such as key types
avoidWhen: Do not plan disk from raw column widths
Do not assume an index is small because its key is
Do not ignore replicas, backups and log space
Do not trust an estimate you could measure with a sample

numbers.title: From table size to recovery time
assumptions: Restore speed: about 200 MB a second
steps: Copy time: 80,000 MB ÷ 200 MB/s = 400 s, about 7 minutes.
Index rebuilds after a logical restore can take as long again or longer.
Replaying a day of logs to reach the right moment adds more time.
At 8 TB the copy alone is about 11 hours, which may be longer than the business can wait.
numbers.result: Size sets recovery time, so a table that grows tenfold needs its recovery plan revisited too.

india.title: PostgreSQL page layout documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual documents the page layout: a 24-byte page header, an array of 4-byte item identifiers pointing to items, free space, and the items themselves. It states that every table row begins with a fixed-size header occupying 23 bytes on most machines, followed by an optional null bitmap, and that values are aligned according to their type.

pitfalls.trap: “The data is 35 GB, so a 50 GB disk is fine”
pitfalls.say: Add overhead, indexes, copies and headroom; measure a sample

pitfalls.trap: Booleans and bigints mixed at random
pitfalls.say: Order columns widest first in PostgreSQL to avoid padding

pitfalls.trap: Estimating an index as key bytes × rows
pitfalls.say: Add the entry header and divide by how full the pages are

takeaways: Bytes per row = data + header + pointer + padding
Index size = entries × entry width ÷ page fill
Indexes often add half the table size or more
Multiply for copies, add headroom, and confirm with a measured sample

interactive.title: Space taken by NULL
interactive.prompt: A PostgreSQL row has a nullable 8-byte bigint column, and it is NULL in this row. How much space does that column use in the row?

choices.label: 8 bytes, the same as any bigint
choices.feedback: NULL values are not stored as data at all.

choices.label: One bit in the row's null bitmap
choices.feedback: Right: a NULL is recorded as a bit, and no bytes are reserved for the value.

choices.label: 4 bytes for a NULL marker
choices.feedback: There is no 4-byte marker; the bitmap holds one bit per column.

interactive.reveal: Sparse nullable columns are cheap in PostgreSQL. The bitmap appears only in rows that contain a NULL, and it is part of the header area.

title: Timeouts and Guardrails Inside the Database
objectives: Explain why client timeouts do not stop work on the server
Set statement, lock and idle-transaction limits per workload
Handle what a timeout leaves behind in a transaction

cards.title: The database needs its own limits
cards.body: A client timeout ends the client's wait; it does not necessarily stop the query. The server may keep running it until it finishes or notices the connection is gone, using CPU, I/O and locks for an answer nobody will read. Server-side limits stop that work. PostgreSQL has statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and, from version 17, transaction_timeout. MySQL has max_execution_time for SELECT statements and innodb_lock_wait_timeout, 50 seconds by default. SQL Server has SET LOCK_TIMEOUT. Together they put a ceiling on how much one session can hold.

cards.title: Worked example: abandoned queries pile up
cards.body: Illustrative figures: 20 requests a second hit a query that suddenly takes 60 seconds; clients give up after 5 seconds and retry once.
steps: Each request runs the query twice: the first attempt and one retry
Without a server limit, each attempt runs the full 60 s, so about 20 × 2 × 60 = 2,400 queries are running at once
That is far beyond the connection limit and CPU, so every other query slows down too
With statement_timeout = 5 s, each attempt stops at 5 s: about 20 × 2 × 5 = 200 at once
Users still see errors, but the database stays up for everyone else while the slow query is fixed

cards.title: Choosing values per workload
cards.body: One global value rarely fits. A web request with a 2-second deadline wants a statement limit at or just under that deadline, because work after the deadline is wasted. A nightly report may legitimately run for 20 minutes. Set limits per role, per database or per transaction (SET LOCAL in PostgreSQL), and give long jobs their own role or a replica. Keep lock_timeout short, a few seconds, for web traffic and schema changes, so a blocked statement fails fast instead of queueing behind a lock.

cards.title: Idle sessions that hold things
cards.body: A session that opened a transaction and then waits on the application, say for an external API call, holds its locks and its snapshot while doing nothing. Other writers queue behind its locks, and in MVCC engines cleanup cannot remove row versions it might still see. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout in PostgreSQL ends such sessions after a set time. The better fix is in the code: do slow external calls before or after the transaction, never inside it. Separate settings close sessions that are idle outside a transaction, such as idle_session_timeout in PostgreSQL 14 and later or wait_timeout in MySQL.

cards.title: Trap: relying on the client timeout alone
cards.body: An application sets a 3-second timeout in its driver and assumes no query can run longer. When the timeout fires, the driver stops waiting; depending on the driver, it may or may not send a cancel request, and the server may keep working. Retries then add more copies of the same expensive query. Set a matching limit on the server as well, and make retries back off.

cards.title: Edge case: what a timeout leaves behind
cards.body: Engines differ in how much a timeout undoes. In PostgreSQL, a statement cancelled by statement_timeout inside a transaction puts the whole transaction into an aborted state: later statements fail until you roll back. In MySQL, innodb_lock_wait_timeout by default rolls back only the statement that waited, and the transaction stays open with its earlier changes; innodb_rollback_on_timeout changes that to a full rollback. Either way, the application must decide: roll back and retry the whole transaction, which must be safe to repeat, or report the failure.

questions.prompt: A client's 3-second timeout fires while its query runs. The server has no statement limit. What happens to the query?

choices.label: It is cancelled on the server at the same moment
It is rolled back and retried by the database
It may keep running until it ends or the server notices
It is paused until the client reconnects

questions.explanation: The timeout ends the client's wait. Unless the driver sends a cancel, the server keeps executing until it finishes or detects the closed connection, often when it tries to send results. Databases do not retry statements on their own, and there is no pause-and-resume for a disconnected client.

questions.prompt: Requests arrive at 30 per second, and each starts a query that now takes 40 seconds on the server. With no server-side limit, about how many of these queries are running at the same moment?
questions.formula: arrival rate × time each one runs (Little's law)
questions.workedAnswer: 30 per second × 40 s = 1,200 running at once
questions.explanation: Design implication: a 4-second statement limit would cut that to 30 × 4 = 120, and the server stays usable while the slow query is fixed. 120 is that capped figure, and 30 is the arrival rate, not the number running.

questions.prompt: A session opened a transaction, updated a row, then waited 10 minutes on an external API. Which setting ends such sessions?

choices.label: statement_timeout
lock_timeout
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
TCP keepalive on the connection

questions.explanation: The session is idle inside a transaction, which is exactly what this setting limits; it ends the session and releases its locks. statement_timeout applies while a statement runs, and none is running. lock_timeout limits waiting for a lock, not holding one. Keepalives detect dead connections, and this one is alive.

questions.prompt: In MySQL with default settings, a statement fails with a lock wait timeout midway through a transaction. What has been undone?

choices.label: Only that statement; earlier changes remain
The whole transaction, back to its start
Nothing; the statement keeps waiting
The whole session, which is disconnected

questions.explanation: By default InnoDB rolls back just the statement that timed out; the transaction is still open with its earlier changes, and the application must decide to roll back or continue. innodb_rollback_on_timeout makes it a full rollback. The statement does stop waiting, and the connection remains open.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a statement inside a transaction hits statement_timeout. Order what follows in a well-behaved application.

items.label: The transaction is now aborted; further statements fail
It retries the whole transaction with backoff, if safe to repeat
The statement is cancelled with an error
The application issues ROLLBACK

questions.explanation: After the error, the transaction cannot continue in PostgreSQL; rolling back clears it, and only a whole-transaction retry can redo the work consistently. Retrying just the failed statement would fail again with "current transaction is aborted".

questions.prompt: An API has a 2-second deadline for each request. What statement limit fits its database role?

choices.label: 30 seconds, to be safe
None, so slow queries still finish
About 1.5 to 2 seconds
50 ms, for every role in the database

questions.explanation: Work that continues past the request deadline is wasted, so the limit should sit at or just under it. 30 seconds lets abandoned queries run 15 times longer than anyone waits. No limit is the pile-up case. 50 ms for every role would break legitimate reports and migrations.

questions.prompt: One PostgreSQL database serves an API with a 2-second deadline and nightly reports that take up to 20 minutes.
constraints: Protect the API from runaway queries

approaches.label: One global limit of 2 s
approaches.description: statement_timeout = 2s for everyone

approaches.label: No limits
approaches.description: Rely on client timeouts and monitoring

approaches.label: Limits per role
approaches.description: API role 2 s; report role 30 minutes, ideally on a replica

rationaleOptions.label: Each workload gets a limit that matches its own deadline
A single global value is easiest and fits both
Reports keep running, but away from the API's connections
Client timeouts already stop server work

rationaleConflicts.r3: A 2-second global limit kills every report; a 20-minute one protects nothing for the API.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A client timeout ends the wait, not necessarily the query on the server.

questions.explanation: Per-role settings cost one ALTER ROLE each and let both workloads have limits that make sense.

flashcards.back: Stops waiting; the server may keep working
Caps how long one statement may run on the server
Caps how long a statement may wait for a lock
Holds locks and snapshot; limit it and keep external calls outside

mechanism.title: What each guardrail measures and what it does when it fires
steps: A statement limit starts a timer when a statement begins. If the statement is still running when it expires, the server cancels it and returns an error; locks it took are released when the transaction ends.
A lock-wait limit starts a timer only while a statement waits for a lock. It turns an indefinite queue into a fast, clear failure, which matters most for schema changes and hot rows.

An idle-in-transaction limit measures time between statements inside an open transaction. When it fires, the server ends the session, which rolls the transaction back and frees its locks and snapshot.
A transaction limit, where available, caps the whole transaction however its time is split between statements and idle gaps.
Idle-session and connection limits close connections that have done nothing for a long time, protecting the connection count rather than locks.
The application sees an error in every case. It must roll back if the engine has not, decide whether the transaction is safe to retry, and back off so retries do not recreate the overload.

useWhen: Every role used by interactive traffic
Schema migrations on busy tables (short lock waits)
Applications that call external services near transactions
Shared databases with mixed workloads
avoidWhen: Do not set one global limit for very different workloads
Do not set statement limits longer than anyone waits
Do not retry immediately and without limit after a timeout
Do not treat a guardrail as the fix for a slow query

numbers.title: Why limits keep an incident small
steps: No limit: 50 × 30 = 1,500 queries would need to run at once, five times the connection limit.
New connections are refused and healthy requests fail too.
With a 2 s limit: 50 × 2 = 100 at once, a third of the connections.
Only the affected endpoint fails, and the rest of the application keeps working.
numbers.result: A server-side limit turns a database-wide outage into one failing endpoint.

india.title: PostgreSQL client connection defaults
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual documents statement_timeout as aborting any statement that takes more than the specified time, lock_timeout as aborting any statement that waits longer than the specified time while attempting to acquire a lock, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as terminating any session that has been idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified time. It advises against setting statement_timeout globally in postgresql.conf because it would affect all sessions, which is the reason to set it per role or per session instead.

pitfalls.trap: “The driver timeout protects the database”
pitfalls.say: It protects the caller; set server-side limits too

pitfalls.trap: One timeout for API and reports
pitfalls.say: Set limits per role or per transaction

pitfalls.trap: Calling an external API inside a transaction
pitfalls.say: Move the call outside; limit idle-in-transaction time as a backstop

takeaways: Client timeouts end the wait, not necessarily the work
Statement, lock-wait and idle-transaction limits each cap a different resource
Match each limit to the deadline of the workload using it
After a timeout, roll back and retry the whole transaction, with backoff

interactive.title: After the timeout
interactive.prompt: In PostgreSQL, inside BEGIN, an UPDATE is cancelled by statement_timeout. The application then runs SELECT 1 in the same transaction. What happens?

choices.label: It returns 1; only the UPDATE failed
choices.feedback: That is closer to MySQL's default for lock-wait timeouts; PostgreSQL aborts the transaction.

choices.label: It fails: the transaction is aborted until ROLLBACK
choices.feedback: Right: every statement fails with "current transaction is aborted" until the transaction ends.

choices.label: The UPDATE is retried automatically first
choices.feedback: The database never retries statements on its own.

interactive.reveal: Code that catches a timeout must end the transaction before doing anything else on that connection, and connection pools should reset sessions they get back in this state.
